en: Commentary on the *Sifen jieben* (The Four-Part Code of Precepts), Scroll One.
Generally, when one wishes to expound upon the title of a scripture, one first employs a threefold classification, followed by an exegesis according to the text.
Regarding these three gates: the first sets forth the essential tenet, subsumes the teachings, and clarifies their ultimate purpose; the second is the knowledge of the teachings...
The third section, "The Essential Purpose," correctly explains the title of the *Śīla-sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "elevating the essence to encompass the teaching":
although the holy teachings are numerous, they are briefly categorized into three types.
First, the Sūtra Piṭaka;
second, the Vinaya Piṭaka;
third, the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
What is called *sūtra* refers to the various discourses (*sūtras*).
What is called *vinaya* refers to...
That is to say, the various codes of discipline (vinaya); as for what is called Abhidharma,
it refers to the various treatises (śāstra).
Now, this *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* is contained within the Tripiṭaka;
specifically, it is subsumed under the second Piṭaka, the Vinaya.
As for the phrase "knowing the ultimate aim of the teaching":
These precepts are spoken of here in a general sense that encompasses both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thus, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* asks:
"What is called the training in increased virtue (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*)?"
That which is called the increase of virtue, the increase of mind, and the increase of wisdom is termed the training in higher virtue (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*).
This is because both the prohibitions and the prescriptions constitute virtue.
Now, seeking the essence [of the path], we shall distinguish it according to the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*).
Within this training in ethical discipline, there are two analytical sections: first, the method of receiving the precepts;
second, the characteristics of practicing in accordance with those precepts.
As for "receiving the precepts," it refers to the initial arousal of a solemn resolve to sever evil and cultivate goodness.
To establish one's resolve and achieve fulfillment,
to receive the Dharma within the mind and eyes is what constitutes "receiving" (śīla).
As for the phrase "following the precepts":
Feeling arises first, and the mental application (*manasikāra*) subsequently follows in accordance with the nature of that feeling; thus it is called "concomitant" (*anuvartin*).
Regarding these two aspects—feeling and concomitance—each is further divided into two.
As for the two aspects of feeling:
Because the conditioned phenomena that constitute the obstructing dharmas of the precepts cannot arise in isolation,
but only emerge after depending upon causes and relying upon conditions,
the text clarifies the conditions that can give rise to them.
Since there is a condition, there must necessarily be that which is obtained;
therefore, next is the second [category], the substance of the precepts produced through the act of receiving.
Regarding the term "condition for receiving":
This is because their status distinguishes between the holy and the ordinary, their retribution differs between male and female, and the conditions upon which they rely are not the same.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* distinguishes five ways of receiving the precepts;
the first is called "welcoming arrival" (*svāgata*).
The second is called the Superior Dharma;
the third is named the Three Refuges;
and the fourth is termed the Eight Teachings.
The fifth is *karmavācanā*.
These five names are fully explained as in the standard commentaries.
Regarding the second point, "receiving the essence":
To summarize, there are no more than two types:
first, the precept of action (vijñapti-śīla);
second, the precept of non-action (avijñapti-śīla).
Regarding what is called "active precept" (*kriyā-śīla*):
it refers to the physical and verbal engagement in purposeful activity and undertaking;
this is termed "action."
Second, there is no agent.
First, the four minds and three natures manifest in a continuous succession from beginning to end;
they are eternally present without depending on conditions.
The analysis of the characters states that it is "non-action" (wu-uo).
These two types both possess a preventive function from afar;
thus, they are equally designated as "precepts" (jie).

If one were to define the *vijñapti* (manifest) precept as having form (*rūpa*) as its essence, then it would follow that the *avijñapti* (unmanifest) precept is neither form nor mind. Second, regarding the analysis of the secondary precepts (*anuvyañjana-śīla*), there are two gates;
the first concerns being single-mindedly diligent and not transgressing.
The second type is one who, having committed an offense, is able to repent;
those called "diligent" belong to the class of superior practitioners.
Superficially following the teachings by abandoning evil and practicing virtue is called "exclusive application," yet this involves only two aspects.
First, it clarifies the observance through restraint;
second, it clarifies the observance through performance.
Regarding what is called "observance through restraint":
Mindfulness, wisdom, equanimity, and so forth carefully guard the body against the commission of various evils;
this is termed "cessation" (śamatha).
Because one maintains cessation without violating [the precepts] and remains pure in receiving [sensory objects], it is called "observance through cessation" (śamathādhiṣṭhāna).
Regarding "active observance" (kriyā-dhāraṇa): it refers to following and conforming to the holy teachings,
performing rituals and activities, and performing the appropriate rites in accordance with specific circumstances.
This is termed "action. Because one acts and subsequently undergoes the consequences, it is called "upholding through action.
Second, regarding those who, having committed an offense, are able to repent:
Those who are not careful allow their bodies and speech to run wild, violating prohibitions and giving rise to transgressions.
Failing to cultivate wholesome deeds and defiling that which they have originally received is termed "offense."
Through shame and remorse, one repents and returns to the original state;
this is also called "maintaining.
Although it is not a case of immediate and perfect accomplishment, it nevertheless involves repairing what was damaged.
The second is called an offense because it is a white dharma;
once one has been able to repent, it is maintained as such.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of offenses.
First is the transgression of commission:
manifesting opposition to the holy teachings and extensively creating various faults is termed the transgression of commission.
The second is the transgression of cessation (*śamatha*).
This refers to failing to comply with the instructions for the cultivation of cessation and thereby violating them;
hence it is called the transgression of cessation.
Regarding these two types of offenses, if one repents and returns to the state of purity,
both are termed "observing" [the precepts].
Thus far, the fundamental tenets of the teaching have been elucidated.
It is precisely because there is feeling that there is following; if there were no feeling, then formations would have nothing from which to arise.
Because feeling exists, the various formations are able to be produced.
If there were no following of formations, there would be faults such as the weakening of the precepts.
Because they are accompanied [by these two], they cause the precepts to be received as radiant and pure.
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"These two kinds of precepts encompass immeasurable other pure precepts."
Therefore, one must accept the two dharmas that follow. Within the gateway of "acceptance" (*vedanā*), the substance of conditions is explained in detail:
first, the condition of acceptance is clarified;
subsequently, the substance of acceptance itself is analyzed.
Regarding the phrase "conditioned by sensation" (*vedanā-pratyaya*),
there is an explanation of its meaning through eight sections.
First is the explanation of the name.
Second, the general and specific meanings of the interpretation;
third, the distinction between the ranks of the masters and disciples who uphold the teaching;
fourth, those for whom the teaching is intended.
The fifth [point] concerns the inequality between the noble ones and ordinary beings;
the sixth distinguishes the timing at which these various conditions give rise to the precepts.
Seventh, the upholding of the sudden and gradual [teachings];
eighth, the comparative evaluation of their superiority and inferiority. Regarding the first, the explanation of names:
the various schools establish these names with varying degrees of frequency.
Some establish four types of feeling and speak of the unsurpassed Dharma;
others establish six types of feeling and, within the discipline (*vinaya*), include among the eight types of bhikṣus those who merely claim to be bhikṣus.
This refers to the meaning of receiving the precepts through self-vow rather than [through formal ordination].
Now, based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, five modes of reception are established.
As for these five modes of reception:
These refer to the "Come hither" (Ehi), the "Superior Dharma" (Uttarimanussa-dhamma), the Three Refuges, the Eight Precepts of Respect, the formal ritual (Kamma), and so forth.
Regarding the term "Come hither":
this person has planted excellent causes in past lives and possesses deep roots of the Path.
Later, he heard the Buddha’s teaching and was deeply moved;
realizing that the fruit of the first stage involves profound weariness with birth and death and a longing to seek renunciation,
he said to the Buddha:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu," is said because the category of precepts arises immediately; thus it is called "Welcome.
Alternatively, these individuals deeply loathe birth and death and long for the renunciation of the household life;
when the Buddha commands them to come, their full ordination arises instantly, and thus it is called "Welcome."
Regarding what is called the "supreme dharma" (agradharma):
it is the principle of the fixed nature that transcends all characteristics;
because no entity can surpass it, it is termed the supreme dharma.
Kāśyapa, free from desire, cultivated the path and advanced in virtue;
as his delusions were exhausted and his understanding fulfilled, he attained the higher dharma and received full ordination.
Therefore, it is called the "higher dharma."

Furthermore, because one may also obtain the precepts by emerging from the "table of the knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*) and entering the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is called the "superior dharma.
Therefore, in the *Mātṛkā-sūtra*, the attainment of full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the superior roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) is established.
Regarding the "three refuges," these people have not yet been moved by the Tathāgata’s profound awakening and vision of the Path;
they merely speak of taking refuge in the various small sages, such as the Arhats.
Thinking this to be a profound auspicious connection, he grew deeply weary of the three realms of existence and aspired to leave the household life.
His mother said,
"The various arhats have instructed him to shave his head and don the dyed robes."
Relying upon the Three Jewels, the mind of taking refuge is fully realized as soon as it arises;
therefore, it is called "the Three Refuges" and designated by "the Three Utterances."
Regarding the "Eightfold Respectful Precepts":
the Buddha suppressed women and did not permit them to enter the Path.
When Pajāpatī heard this, she gave rise to a sense of weary detachment.
He then shaved his own head and stood leaning against the Jeta Grove.
Upon seeing him, Ānanda made three requests on his behalf,
and the Tathāgata proclaimed from afar the reverence due to the Dharma.
Ānanda transmitted [the teachings].
When Āmrapālī heard this,
she held these eight dharmas in high esteem and, with the intention of practicing them, immediately attained full ordination.
Therefore, it is called the "Eight Respects.
As for what is termed *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action),
such individuals must rely upon powerful external conditions.
Only by supporting those weak causes can the conditions for generating the precepts be activated.

When the monastic community pronounces the *karmavācanā*, the category of the precepts is generated; the capacity of the officiant is concealed, and the name is designated according to that which is being undertaken.

Therefore, it is said that there is the "ordination through *karmavācanā*. Regarding these five methods of receiving the precepts, there are four ways in which they receive their names: [the ordination by] "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*), and [the others] are distinguished by their essence and their objective sphere.
"Wholesome" refers to the practitioner's mind seeking the precepts;
since this is the sacred teaching,
the delusions [of such a mind] may be praised, and thus it is called "receiving the precepts with a mind."
The Buddha said, "Welcome," and thus it was so.
The superior dharma is derived from its object; furthermore, it may be received according to its essential nature. This is what is meant by the establishment of the name "reception" (vedanā).
Because the roots of goodness receive full ordination at the highest level—
namely, the two types of reception [of precepts] through the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising;
this is determined by way of both the object and the mind.
Karma follows from instruction;
it may also be considered a merit, as it is defined by the settlement of matters. Second, the general and the specific.
The four types of formal acceptance (*caturvidha-samādāna*) are the particulars, while the ritual act (*karmavācanā*) is the general category;
the name is established based on its remote cause.
Whether four or six, they are called "comprehensive" because the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) encompasses them all. Question:
Since there are four conditions for receiving the precepts through the *karmavācanā*, [why is it so?]
For what reason is only the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) specifically highlighted, while the others are not given specific names?
One explanation states:
Names are manifested through various other conditions;
for now, setting aside the specific and relying on the general, we designate it as "karmavācanā" (formal ritual action).
How could this be considered an obstacle? Regarding the third point, the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya* states:
The [first] is attained by oneself through the vision of the truths;
the remaining six are derived from others,
because they are explained in contrast to the seven types of feeling.
Now, judging these five by analogy with that treatise from a broad perspective,
they all derive from the Buddha,
because it is through the appearance of a Buddha in the world that this Dharma exists.
If one infers according to the underlying principle,
receiving the precepts through the aforementioned method is called "self-receiving," while the remaining four types are obtained from others.
How is it that the superior dharmas are called "self-experienced"?
The treatise states:
"In terms of the fundamental [attainment]."
Because one attains realization of the untainted (anāsrava) through the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma and brings it to fulfillment,
it is called "receiving from the Buddha.
This is inferred by way of its meaning.
One attains full ordination through the clear manifestation of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) within oneself;
it is also called "attained by oneself" rather than "received from another.
Thus, the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* states:
If "dharma" refers to the five bhikṣus who received [the teachings] from the Teacher and others,
then why does the treatise state that it is "attained through the instruction of another"? Answer:
This is stated according to the remote cause.
The "Welcome" and the "Eightfold Respectful Precepts" are what the Buddha himself upheld and are said to have been received from the Buddha.

The *triśaraṇa-karman* (three-refuge ritual) is that which disciples receive; thus it is called "respect received from a disciple. The fourth [category] is the classification of those who are the objects of these [precepts].
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the "ordination by the 'Come, monk' formula" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) is restricted to those at the stage of an *ārya*.
Thus, the Vinaya states:
"Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and realized the fruit, one thereafter attains untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*)."
Having left the household life out of a mind of wearying detachment— the very height of compliance—
he was then met with the words "Welcome," whereupon he received the full precepts.
From the stage of the inner ordinary person (antarapudgala) downward, the mind associated with conceptualization hears [the teaching],
yet it does not reach the ultimate state of conformity;
therefore, it lacks the capacity for crossing over.
Furthermore, regarding the higher formal undertaking (*adhi-dharma-samādāna*):
it necessarily pertains to the fourth fruit (*caturtha-phala*), because its exhaustion, understanding, and fulfillment are complete.
This includes the three refuges (*tri-śaraṇa*) and the eight precepts of respect (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*), which apply from the level of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) upward.
For this reason, many treatises state that these two methods of receiving the precepts are neither weakened nor abandoned;
thus we know that from the stage of the inner ordinary person (*antarapudgala*) onward,
they are referred to as "receiving through ritual action" (*karmavācanā*).
At the beginning, [the practice] was for ordinary people;
after one person had attained realization, it was universally applied to three types of individuals,
just as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, where the brahmin of pure conduct attained the first fruit.
The formal act (*karmavācanā*) has already been performed for the conferral [of the precepts].
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the case of the nun Utpalavarṇā is also similar to this example. Fifth, regarding the requisites for the "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣuṇī*) ordination: it is complete.
Through four conditions, one attains the first fruit of realization.
The text states:
"Having seen the Dharma and attained the Dharma," there was previously a wholesome mind of renunciation.
The scriptural text states:
"Because they wish to practice the holy life within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, the three provisional forms manifest before the Buddha’s form.
The text says:
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"There are four provisional Buddhist teachings;
that is to say, the noble command 'Come,' the higher dharma, and receiving the precepts—these three conditions give rise to [the path]."
First, receiving instruction from a provisional Buddha,
as described in the *Abhidharmadīpa*.
Second, possessing a mind that seeks the precepts.
Therefore, in other texts, it is stated that because Arhats and Śrāmaṇeras lack the intention to renounce the world,
they can only attain the fruit [of their practice] if they possess the requisite mind.
Third, they attain the untainted realization of emptiness.
This means that when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests, one immediately attains full ordination (*upasaṃpad*).
Receiving the precepts through the threefold formula also possesses three conditions:
first, a formal disciple; second, a physical presence; and third, a Dharma-Arhat.
Second is the teaching for nominal disciples:
this refers to one who receives the three refuges with complete verbal formulae;
because they have fully internalized the preceding refuges through a mind of threefold refuge, they are able to obtain the precepts.
The observance of the eight precepts of respect arises from four conditions:
first, the provisional teaching of the Buddha regarding the eight respects;
second, the provisional form of a disciple.
Third is the instruction for the disciples,
which refers to the oral proclamation of the meaning of the Eight Respectful Precepts and the Four Practices; thus,
Mahāprajāpatī presented her own petition.
We accept this upon our heads.
The full ordination through the *karmavācanā* possesses four conditions,
as explained in the Vinaya.
First, the condition for the fulfillment of the number of monks;
second, the condition for the accomplishment of the teaching;
third, the condition for the accomplishment of the boundary demarcation.
There are four conditions that do not obstruct the body.
If one possesses these four, a great bhikṣu succeeds in establishing the root of the precepts.
One who violates the precepts and lacks even one of these four is not a great bhikṣu.
One becomes a bhikṣu by following these four directions. Question:
Receptions such as "Welcome" (Svāgata) take the mind as their condition;
why is it that the single reception through formal ritual (karmavācanā) is not likewise? Answer:
The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is not devoid of mental intention;
however, because it employs provisional external conditions to perform the rite and establishes it through forceful determination, the name of its underlying cause is subsumed.
Furthermore, it may also be that through the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), all four types of mind are simultaneously acquired;
however, fearing confusion and a failure to distinguish the objects of those minds,
this is also based on the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*.
Fourth, it takes the mind as its object.
Although the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for the single undertaking is not explicitly listed in the text,
it must nonetheless involve the mind.
According to the Vinaya texts, those who are asleep, insane, or otherwise mentally deranged cannot receive the precepts. Sixth, regarding the timing of receiving the precepts:
for one who receives them by the "Come hither" (Ehi-bhikkhu) formula, full ordination is attained immediately upon the completion of the proclamation "Come hither."
Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"It continues until it is exhausted.
If one follows the original method, it is attained when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests at the time of receiving the precepts.

According to the criteria of the Hīnayāna, for an Arhat whose holy life (*brahmacarya*) is established, because their ethical discipline (*śīla*) is naturally pure, they no longer receive the precepts from another. Question:
Does one who has attained this superior dharma attain both manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*)? Answer: [Yes].
Because it is a non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), one merely obtains the non-manifest. Question:
Since it is not a manifest precept (*vijñapti-śīla*), by what cause is the non-manifest precept produced? Answer:
Because it is not a training (śaikṣa), there is no formal act (kriyā).
By the power of the Path, one obtains the precept of non-action (akriyā-śīla).
Upon the completion of the third utterance of the three refuges for receiving the precepts, the full precepts (upasaṃpadā) are immediately produced.
The eighth [section], the exposition on receiving the precepts through the eight respects, concludes here; this constitutes the Chapter on Attaining the Precepts.
Upon the completion of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for the first reception, one immediately generates full ordination (*upasampadā*).
This is largely consistent with various treatises. Section Seven concerns the gradual and instantaneous aspects of receiving and relinquishing [the precepts].
First, to clarify the gradual and sudden ways of receiving [the precepts]:
the single reception through *karmavācanā* is both gradual and sudden;
the remaining four types of reception are sudden, not gradual.
Regarding the gradual and sudden approaches:
in the gradual *karmavācanā*, one first receives the five precepts, next receives the ten precepts,
and finally receives full ordination.
This is called the gradual method.
If one does not receive the fifty precepts but receives the full ordination directly, one obtains the three types of precepts.
It is said that this constitutes an instantaneous [receiving]. Question:
If one can receive the three types of precepts simultaneously, why is it necessary to receive them gradually? Answer:
To cultivate and study the Buddha-dharma, one must necessarily follow a sequential order.
First, one receives the five precepts to bring oneself under discipline;
thus, faith and delight gradually increase.
Next, upon receiving the ten precepts, their wholesome mind becomes increasingly profound;
next, they receive full ordination.
In this manner, they gradually attain the flavor of the Buddha-dharma.
One who delights in firmness may fall back, yet does not lose the sequence [of practice] nor break the dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*).
It is like entering the great ocean, gradually going deeper.
One who receives [the teachings] all at once loses both the sequence and that dignified demeanor.
Therefore, one must receive them gradually. Question:
For one who receives the three precepts all at once, is the essence of their non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) one or three? Answer: *The provided text ends here.*

However, when the complete precepts are undertaken, there is only one substance of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), and no other two substances of non-informative action exist. If this is so, then since it is but a single precept, how can one speak of three? Answer:
When a bhikṣu receives the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) that prevents killing,
it is identical in its essential substance to that of a śrāmaṇera or a layperson who shares the same precepts.
Therefore, many masters of the treatises rely on their essential nature;
looking at the distinct stages from beginning to end for the three types of persons, they say that one obtains three separate precepts.
In reality, however, there are not three. Question:
How do we know that there is only one [type of precept] and not three? Answer:
It is because this very treatise, in its explanation of the sequential reception [of precepts], states that for a layperson, there is the lower grade of the five precepts.
Next, regarding the middle-grade mind, one receives the five precepts of the śrāmaṇera ordination; these remain essentially the same as the lower-grade five precepts,
but because they are generated beyond the mere five precepts, they constitute the middle grade.
Regarding the higher grade of mind for receiving full ordination, the first two grades are still considered lower and middle;
it is only when one emerges from the fifty [days] of the lower and middle grades that it becomes the higher grade.
Based on these two proofs, one receives the precepts gradually in successive order.
The three periods of time differ in their mental states, yet the non-informative action (avijñapti) of the same precept does not arise in three ways.
How much less could there be three [types of non-informative action] for a single person who receives the precepts at different times?
Therefore, we know that the three are established as distinct based on the differences in the stages of gradual progression.
It is also acceptable to say that there are not three distinct entities.
The *Cittaviparyāsa-śāstra* states:
"All causes and all factors obtain the three types of precepts."
One gradually receives [the precepts] over three periods.
Since the times of receiving them are distinct,
and because the non-informative (avijñapti) karma arises repeatedly with three distinct entities, [the precepts are established].

If we discuss sudden reception, since the reception occurs all at once, it can only be said that there are three stages in terms of their relative positions; it is not that there are three distinct entities. Next, I shall explain the gradual and sudden aspects of relinquishing them.
If one looks toward the four types of formal acts (*kamma*), the receiving and relinquishing are both simultaneous;
however, the relinquishing through formal act contains both gradual and simultaneous aspects.
Is it then only a single reception through formal act?
Regarding the gradual relinquishing of the constraints of both the gradual and sudden [approaches]: Question.
Since one has already obtained the three precepts through the sudden reception of the *karmavācanā*, how does one relinquish them? Answer.
The meaning encompasses both the gradual and the sudden.
If, in essence, one abandons all three precepts simultaneously, then all three are lost at once;
this is called "sudden abandonment."

If one says, "I am a śrāmaṇera and thus merely relinquish the full precepts," or says, "I am an upāsaka and thus further relinquish the ten precepts," or says, "I am a person of the Three Refuges and thus relinquish the five precepts," this is called gradual and sudden. Question: [What is the meaning of this?]
Regarding acceptance and relinquishment, both may be simultaneous or gradual;
alternatively, one may accept gradually and relinquish suddenly—
these three cases are possible.
If one originally received [the precepts] all at once and obtained only the single substance of full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), how could it be gradually relinquished?
If it were to be gradually relinquished, it would then consist of three substances.
Question: How can it be said that they are one? Answer:

When a bhikṣu at one time undertakes the restraint against killing, the non-informative action (avijñapti) is common to śrāmaṇeras and laypeople alike; they all share in the restraint against wrongdoing.
Therefore, at the time of relinquishing, one must do so with the intention;
even if the ten precepts are not fully relinquished,
if they are maintained in common with the śrāmaṇera precepts, they remain as long as the intention persists.
Therefore, the Vinaya text states:
"I am a śrāmaṇera. The meaning of the ten [precepts] being paired with the five is likewise the same.
Hence it is said.
I am an upāsaka; therefore, the treatise explains that based on the essential nature, this meaning is common to all three types of persons.
Thus, with respect to their respective positions, it speaks of three.
The substance is not threefold.
When explained in this manner, there is no way to prevent the implications that one would either abandon all at once or adopt gradually;
thus, [the view] is as numerous as the leaves on a tree.
In summer it is green, in autumn yellow, and in winter it is white.
Is it that the substance itself differs?
Rather, because they change according to the seasons, the colors of the tree leaves differ.
Yet from beginning to end it remains a single leaf;
the precepts are likewise thus:
they are always a single precept that varies according to the stage.
Therefore, regarding the single reception of the *karmavācanā*,
both the reception and the relinquishment may be either simultaneous or gradual;
however, the four methods such as "Come hither" (*ehi-bhikṣu*) are exclusively simultaneous and not gradual.

Because they are abandoned by means of non-conditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the eighth [point] regarding their relative superiority or inferiority is as explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
If one considers the presence or absence of calamities and afflictions,
the four types of feeling (*vedanā*) are superior.
The *karman* (ritual procedure) is inferior;
if one takes up the support of the Buddha-dharma for the sake of vast and long-lasting benefit,
the *karman* alone is superior.
The other four types of ordination are inferior.
Regarding the statement that "four are superior and one is inferior," the one who receives the *karmavācanā* ordination is in reality still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Those with meager merit receive this precept;
they are subject to many calamities and may feel weary of the higher realms while longing for the lower ones,
such that their resolve to uphold it is weak.
This causes the precepts to become weak.
Regarding the remaining four methods of receiving the Dharma, from the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) onward,
one receives and attains these precepts within the understanding of the mind.
First, they maintain a firm mind,
being robust rather than emaciated.
Second, ordinary persons engaged in ritual action (karmavācanā) may have a lack of joy for the Dharma and abandon what they originally received.
Regarding the remaining four who receive the Dharma with a sincere mind and a path of joy, it is logically impossible for them to retreat or abandon it.
Third, in the case of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), there may be the possibility of one’s gender changing to become both male and female;
however, for the remaining four who receive the Dharma, such a transformation does not occur.

Fourth, regarding the four types of *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) for receiving [the precepts]: one who receives them through *karmavācanā* may give rise to wrong views and sever their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
The other four types of understanding do not sever the roots of goodness.
Because the single instance of receiving via *karmavācanā* may involve the aforementioned four [defects], it is termed "inferior" (*hīna*).
The other four types of feeling do not possess the aforementioned fault;
therefore, they are called "superior.
This is contrasted with those that first arise.
If a noble one receives [the precepts], this too is superior.
Regarding the statement that "one is superior while four are inferior," the single reception through *karmavācanā* possesses six meanings.
First, its duration is long,
meaning it extends through both the present and the future.
Second, it abides pervasively throughout the three directions.
Excluding the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, whose retribution includes both males and females;
these four stages encompass both ordinary beings and sages;
and the fifth category comprises those who are infinite in number.
Sixth is the procedure for sitting in assembly.

Based on these various principles, the beginning and end of the Buddha-dharma take the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) as its fundamental core.
It is able to continue the Three Jewels and bring about boundless benefit.
Since there is no function of sustaining [the Dharma] greater than that of karma (karmavācanā),
it is said to be supreme.
Among the remaining four types of reception (*vedanā*), the single reception of "Welcome" (*svāgata*) reached its ultimate end at the Twin Śāla Trees;
the other three receptions ceased midway.
Furthermore, this was restricted to Jambudvīpa and did not encompass the other two continents.

In general, the distinctions between the stages of ordinary beings and sages, as well as the limitations of their retributions regarding gender, result in mutual deficiencies when compared to the aforementioned six meanings;
because they lack the merit and evidence for succession [to Buddhahood], they are termed the "four inferiorities."
The section on the conditions for generating the precepts is concluded. Second, the essence of the received [precepts] is analyzed.
Within this, there are four sections for systematic examination.
First: explaining the names and identifying the essence of the two types of precepts, as well as their sequence.
Second, the reception and the similarities and differences;
third, the clarification of the conditions for the arising of the precepts;
fourth, the extent of what is produced. First, regarding the explanation of the names:
Although the characteristics of the precepts are numerous, their essential meaning comprises two types:
first, the active precept (*kriyā-śīla*);
second, the non-active precept (*avijñapti-śīla*).
First, I shall explain the specific names: "action" (karma) and "non-action" (avijñapti).
Next, I will interpret the general name, "precept" (śīla), which is the object referred to.
What is called "action" refers to the initiation and performance of physical and verbal conduct through skillful means.
This is designated as "action.
Thus, the *Cittaviparyāsa-śāstra* states:
"Action is the bodily movement of the agent."

That which is called "non-informative" (avijñapti) refers to the fact that once the bodily movement initiated by an agent has ceased, those dharmas continue to arise in conjunction with subsequent consciousnesses;
this is termed "non-informative," as in the case of having properly received the precepts.
When a defiled or indeterminate state of mind is present, wholesome restraint arises accordingly;
the same applies to unwholesome restraint.
Next, the general meaning of the term "restraint" (*śīla*) will be explained.
Both this manifest action (*kṛta*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) possess the quality of providing preventive restraint; thus, both are collectively termed "precept" (*śīla*).
According to the *Śraddhākaravarman-sūtra* (or *Sujāta-sūtra*), there are five names that apply universally to these.
One name for it is *saṃvara* (restraint).
It is called "precept" (*śīla*) because it restrains and cuts off all that is unwholesome.
It is also called "constriction" (*saṃvṛti*).
Although various evils exist, it is called "precept" (*śīla*) because they cannot be tolerated;
it is also called "cooling," because it obstructs the heat of the afflictions and prevents them from entering.
It is also called "Ascending," for it enables one to ascend to heaven and reach the Unsurpassed Way;
it is also called "Learning."
It is called "precept" (*śīla*) because it tames the mind and intellect;
these five [aspects] are all explanations of the name based on its functional significance.
Therefore, the name is established according to its function.
It is called "precept" (śīla).
However, among the five [aspects], "narrowness" and "coolness" are the meanings of the name, while the remaining three are names based on their function. Question:
How is it known that there are both manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) actions? Answer:
Various treatises extensively clarify two kinds of precept-essence (*śīla-svabhāva*), such as the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (如心論).
At the moment of the third *karmavācanā*, both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) constitute the fundamental path of action (*mūlakarmapatha*).
Furthermore, it is said that the two preceding [moments] of bodily and vocal manifestation are characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*).
The non-manifestations (*avijñapti*) of body and speech are both invisible and non-obstructive.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"In the first moment of the precept, there are both the manifestations (*vijñapti*) and the non-manifestations (*avijñapti*) of body and speech."
In the second moment of thought, there is only non-informative action (*avijñapti*) and no informative action (*vijñapti*).
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states:
"The roots of goodness regarding the meaning of the Vinaya are of two kinds."
The first is the manifest (vijñapti);
the second is the unmanifest (avijñapti).
The manifest is form; the unmanifest is neither form nor mind.
By means of this text, it is clearly understood that there are two kinds of precepts. Question:
Why must one perform the "unmanifest" (avijñapti)? Answer:
If there were no such performance, the unmanifest would have nothing from which it could arise.
If there were no unmanifest action (*avijñapti*), one could not prevent wrongdoing throughout a single lifetime;
therefore, both types of precepts are required. This is merely stated from the perspective of this stage.
Thus, one obtains the precepts through the aforementioned method.
By the power of the Path, one attains the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*). Next, the essence of the precept is distinguished:
according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, both manifest and unmanifest precepts have material form (*rūpa-dharma*) as their essence.
This meaning may be described as sixfold discrimination:
first, the discrimination between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
second, [the discrimination that] morality is a collection of conditioned phenomena, as it is not among the three unconditioned [phenomena].
Second, regarding the three aggregates within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*):
the *karmavācanā* (verbal action) and *akarmavācanā* (non-verbal action) precepts have material form (*rūpa*) as their essence;
the mind (*citta*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), along with non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), [constitute the remaining aggregates].
Because this is the cause of that precept,
the treatise states: "Action and non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) constitute the differentiated aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)."
Within the third aggregate of matter, there is a threefold classification of matter:
first, visible and resistant matter,
which refers to the five sense faculties and the four bases.
Third, there is invisible and non-resistant matter,
which refers to the unmanifest within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
If one says that manifest precepts are subsumed under the first two types of matter, [this is incorrect].
Regarding the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*), because it is subsumed under the third category of form (*rūpa*),
the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Abhidharmanyāyānusāra* state:
"Bodily manifest action (*kāya-vijñapti*) is visible and possesses resistance (*sapratigha*)."
Vocal manifest action is invisible and resistant;
bodily and vocal non-manifest actions are both invisible and non-resistant.
Regarding bodily manifest action among the two aforementioned types of matter, it is subsumed solely within the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
That which constitutes vocal action (vākkarman) is subsumed under the sense-base of sound (śabdāyatana);
the other eight types of form, as well as the two types of non-manifest action (avijñapti), are all subsumed under the sense-base of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Both these manifest and non-manifest actions belong to the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
Fourth, regarding the distinction between the retribution and the application within form and sound:
although form encompasses both retribution and application,
bodily action is an application and not a retribution.
Therefore, the *Cittaviparyāsa-śāstra* states:
"The agent's bodily movement is the bodily expedient;
verbal action is merely the expedient."
Because sound is not a result of retribution (*vipāka-dharma*),
the two types of non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) of body and speech are neither results of retribution nor products of effort (*prayoga*).
Fifth, there is the analysis according to the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
The physical and verbal aspects—color and sound—are virtuous, and not otherwise.
Thus, the *Cittaviveka* states:
"To move the body and speech with a pure mind is called 'wholesome action' (*kuśalakriyā*) and so forth."
Regarding the first category of visible form, there are twenty types.
The first twelve are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta);
the latter eight are high and low, long and short, square and round, regular and irregular.
It encompasses all three natures while specifically taking up the virtuous aspect;
it constitutes the essence of bodily precept-action (*kāya-śīla*).
Among the three types of sound, this refers to excluding the second cause.
The sounds of the four great elements are not perceived [as such], like wind or rain and so forth,
because they are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, one perceives the sounds of the four great elements based on the first cause.
The third reason is the inclusion of the term "sound.
Among these two, which pertain to all three moral natures (*tridharmatā*), the category of wholesome sound is also taken as the essence of vocal action.
Generally speaking, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of both body and speech pertains to both moral natures.
Since this treatise now discusses ethical discipline (*śīla*), it is subsumed under the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala*).
Regarding the sixth [category], the analysis of the beginning and end:
within this wholesome action (*karmasamutthāna*), both the beginning and the end are included, yet the beginning is not taken [as the primary focus].
This refers to the period beginning from the request for a preceptor up until the conclusion of the *karmavācanā*;
as long as the mind has not yet reached maturity,
it is considered "wholesome" but not yet "precept."
The third *karmavācanā* lasts for a single moment;
it requires that the mind be fully satisfied so that the vow may be accomplished as a wholesome state.
However, because this is a formal precept (*śīla*), it is restricted to its conclusion.
However, according to the school that maintains the doctrine of non-informative (avijñapti) precepts,
these are definitively held to have a nature that is neither form nor mind;
as for informative (vijñapti) precepts, the textual sources on their nature are not fixed.
Some take the vocal sound, the physical form, and the mind as its essence;
therefore, the text of the treatise states:
"Karma is not merely vocal sound."
It must be accomplished through the assistance of mental power.
Therefore, one should know that bodily action is also called "accomplished through the assistance of mental power.
It is clearly understood that both types of action have the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) as their essence.
Furthermore, he cites a treatise which takes the mind as its essence.
Thus, the treatise states:
"Apart from the mind, there is no volition, nor are there bodily or vocal actions."
Therefore, it is known that the two types of karma have mental application as their essence,
while they take provisional form as the essence of bodily and vocal karma.
Thus, the treatise says:
The bodily and vocal karmas depend upon the four great elements, while the mental karma depends upon the mind.
If the bodily and vocal karmas did not have the four great elements as their substance, [they would not exist].
It is also not tenable that the nature [of mental action] depends on the mind while having the mind as its substance; rather, because mental action depends on the mind,
it is said that mental action takes the mind as its substance.
Therefore, one should know that the bodily action (kāyakarman) takes the movement of the four great elements (mahābhūta) as its activity.
This action has no separate substance;
it takes the four great elements themselves as its substance.
Regarding vocal action (*vākkarman*): the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are interconnected within which sound is produced.
When this sound forms melodies and tunes that signify specific meanings, it constitutes syllables and phrases; this is what constitutes vocal action.
Karma has no separate substance;
it takes sound as its substance.
Therefore, the treatise says:
This phenomenon is named the nature of sound. Since it is subsumed within the sense-base of mental objects (dharmāyatana),
it is established as sound by being derived from the four great elements at a distance.
Therefore, vocal action has sound as its substance.
Since bodily action closely relies upon the four great elements,
it takes those very supports as its substance.
Next, the sequence of the two types of precepts is explained.
According to the *Cittaviparyāsa-śāstra*, they are as if obtained simultaneously; thus the text says:
The third [view] holds that the first moment constitutes the fundamental course of action (*karmapatha*) consisting of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) [matter].
Furthermore, many say that the precept of the first moment consists of the informative [act], while the non-informative [act] arises subsequently in succession.
In the second moment of mindfulness regarding precepts, there is only non-informative action (*avijñapti*) and no informative action (*vijñapti*).
Thus, one knows that at that single moment there is non-manifest action;
yet, in the three periods of time, there may be that which is not precept.
First, there is non-informative action (*avijñapti*) at the time of the cause;
this is merely that which co-exists with informative action (*vijñapti*) and is not the complete essence of the precept.
Second, there is non-informative action at the time of the fruit, which is the body itself.
There are two kinds of non-manifestation (avijñapti): first, that which is concomitant with action;
second, that which is concomitant with form.
Only that which is simultaneous with the physical form (*rūpa-sahabhū*) is the essence of the precept (*śīla-skandha*).
The third [category] refers to that which follows the fruit and is restricted solely to what is simultaneous with the physical form;
this is the essence of the precept.
Because at the time of its fruition it exists simultaneously with form, it is clarified that it is acquired at one time.
If, however, one follows this school,
it arises sequentially, first and then later.
Thus the *Shi* says:
Question:
To what extent is it designated as "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*)?
Answer: The second moment must be called "non-action" (avijñapti),
because the precept of action (vijñapti-śīla) constitutes the first moment.
The non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) of the second moment is called "nameless" (*anāmakīya*).
Only that which exists once the ritual action (*karmavācanā*) is completed constitutes the essence of this precept (*śīla-svabhāva*).
During the preceding two moments, its status is that of being subsumed by both the agent and the object.

Furthermore, according to the *Suśruta-sūtra*, when the mind of intention (*cetanā*) differs from the mind at the time of action, and various conditions (*pratyaya*) converge, this is designated as "action" (*kriyā*).
Through these causal conditions of action, "non-action" (*avijñapti*) arises.
Once it has been performed and has passed away, there remains only the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*).
Even though the mind may dwell within the unwholesome or the neutral (*avyākṛta*),
the original action that was performed is not called "lost" or "transferred."
Next, this section clarifies the sequence of their arising.

Second, regarding the identity and difference between "receiving" (*samādāna*) and "conforming" (*anuvartana*), the former interpretation held that the meaning of receiving and conforming was one and the same.
To refute this point, it is like a single shield that can select and repel many enemies.
Therefore, these two dharmas—receiving and following—are established as both manifest (vijñapti) and non-manifest (avijñapti).
First, regarding the non-manifest, there are seven types. The first is the non-manifest associated with the Path (mārga-sahagatā avijñapti).
Second, that which is common to both meditative absorptions;
third, that which is simultaneous with physical form; fourth, that which arises from a formal commitment.
For example, [the non-informative action] of a vow regarding day and night or a specific period, and so forth.
Fifth, there is non-informative action that follows karma;
this refers to the non-informative action that follows a precept, as well as that which arises following the informative action of a neutral state.
These six types of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) are like stūpas, monasteries, bridges, boats, and so forth;
while the activity persists, non-informative action arises moment by moment.
Seventh is non-informative action that follows from usage.
Regarding the aforementioned matter, when it occurs in a person who employs [the vow], it arises again even in the absence of an agent.

Among these seven types, the "form-concomitant" (rūpa-sahagata) and the "fixed-to-be-experienced" (niyata-vedanīya) apply to both [types of persons], while the remaining five are necessarily restricted [to one].
Next, the similarities and differences will be distinguished.
There are three identical meanings regarding the reception, the conformity, and the non-manifestation (avijñapti):
namely, name, substance, and meaning.
If these differ, there are six.
Regarding the first [category], the meaning of non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) within the undertaking (*samādāna*) is uniform across a single grade.
It is only within the subsequent [category] that non-manifest action possesses degrees of superiority and inferiority.
As for the statement that non-manifest action within the undertaking constitutes a single grade:
If the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is produced by a superior-grade mental feeling (*citta-vedanā*), then because the mind is predominant,
the precept is also superior-grade; however,
it is possible that one might still commit an offense.
Or, at the very least, one reaches the stage of Arhat without further increase or decrease,
because one has repaid the single grade of the original mind;
the same principle applies to those with middling or inferior minds.
Because each of the three grades is fixed,
their meanings are equal within a single grade. However,
because there is no fixed number of grades according to the intermediate [grade] and because they are indeterminate, there is a distinction of superiority and inferiority.
Regarding the discernment of these five categories of superiority and inferiority:
if one proceeds from the perspective of the roots and branches, the first is superior and the last five are inferior;
if one proceeds from the perspective of one's own stage versus further progress, the latter five are superior and the first is inferior.
This corresponds precisely to the sequential meaning of the five categories [of offenses].
Furthermore, within each category and each individual precept, there may be variations in intensity— ranging from slight to grave—
and as the specific circumstances differ, there are accordingly nine grades of observance.
Therefore, according to the absence of volitional action (avijñapti), there are these successive stages.
In the second [stage], regarding the general and specific undertaking of non-action and the arousal of the mind of awakening,
one universally severs all evil intentions.
Regarding birth, one attains the restraint (saṃvara) instantaneously and not through a gradual process;
therefore, it is called "comprehensive" (sāmānya).
However, the non-manifest action (avijñapti) that follows [the restraint] is established gradually according to its sequence and cannot arise instantaneously.
Therefore, it is called "distinct.
Third, regarding the non-manifest (avijñapti) within the category of restraint, there is already a prevention of wrongdoing even while one has not yet engaged in actual action.
In accordance with [the precepts], one refrains from wrongdoing by guarding against it through non-action;
thus, conduct becomes pure and bright. Question:
Since there is no wrongdoing prior to its occurrence, what is the use of receiving the precepts for the purpose of conforming to conduct? Answer:
If that [primary] sensation were absent, the secondary ones would not be established;
for they are mutually constituted as a single therapeutic treatment.
This is the fourth [point], regarding length and shortness.
This feeling is concomitant with form;
it is described as being "long.
The non-manifesting karma that follows from conduct arises from cultivation and is not concomitant with form.
Therefore, it is designated as "short.

Fifth, regarding the existence or non-existence of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*): it pervades all three natures [wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral], yet is exclusively wholesome.
As for the unmanifest itself, its nature is not dual; thus, it likewise does not pertain to both [the wholesome and unwholesome].
This is based on a classification according to their specific natures;
feeling is wholesome in its concomitance,
while the other two are both restricted.
Now, regarding existence and non-existence, as well as pervasion and non-pervasion:
sensation is a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma) that pervades the other two natures.
Therefore, it is said to be "broad.
It accompanies [the mind] accordingly;
"equality" is restricted to the nature of wholesomeness.
Therefore, it is said to be narrow;
this is stated with reference to one's own mind acting alone.
If, however, it involves preceding and succeeding moments of mind, as well as instructing others, [the scope is broader].
In the remaining two natures, they likewise correspondingly pervade as far as the meanings expressed by the scriptural characteristics allow;
within the categories of transgression and non-transgression, it is similarly restricted in this way.
Therefore, among transgressive actions, there is no action that is not a transgression.
If one considers the transgression in terms of both preceding and succeeding moments of mind as well as instructing another,
there are instances within the commission of an offense where no offense is incurred; thus,
both the primary precept (*śīla*) and its subsequent application (*anuśīla*) are broad in scope.
Those who provide this interpretation must nevertheless establish them as three;
for if they were restricted solely to the nature of the wholesome, they would be too narrow, since feeling (vedanā) and mental concomitants (cetanā) share that same wholesome nature.
If one follows [the view that] persons and so forth are all equally broad,
it is because they are partially applicable to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
If, however, one distinguishes by correlating "acting for oneself" with "following [others]," [it is as follows].
There are variations in their breadth and narrowness;
according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are four or five such differences.
However, according to the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, they do not differ in terms of breadth, narrowness, length, or shortness.
Thereafter, it is certain that the non-manifestation (avijñapti) within the intermediate state is long and wide;
according to the non-manifestation, it possesses both qualities,
for the non-manifestation of the Path is indeed broad and extensive.
Regarding the sixth [topic], the sensations, which are the roots, and their corresponding branches, we shall next explain the similarities and differences between these two functions.
There are five points of similarity:
namely, name, substance, and meaning.
There are four types of differences, such as broad and narrow, long and short; first,
many within each category, and second, the general and the particular.
The third also corresponds by suspension.
The fourth consists of roots and branches;
it can be understood through comparison with what has been explained.

Since there is this distinction, how could it be the same as the former interpretation regarding the meaning of "receiving" (*pratigraha*) and "following" (*anuvartana*)? Third, concerning the analysis of the conditions for the arising of the precepts:
if one follows the Sarvāstivāda school...
The Prātimokṣa precepts apply only to the present,
because the past and future are not sentient beings.
This is according to the tenet regarding their acquisition.
The time of generating the precepts does not lie in a past or future mind,
because the attainment of the precepts does not pertain to non-sentient beings; rather,
the precepts are generated within the continuous stream of the present mind.
Therefore, when sentient beings receive the precepts,
they must form the intention to sever all evils existing within the objects of the three periods of time before the precepts can arise; thus,
they prevent non-virtue regarding the objects of the three periods of time.
The reason for this is that objects of the past can give rise to unwholesome thoughts.
As the treatise states:
Just as a person who makes offerings to those honored in the past also gains merit,
so it is with the restraint (saṃvara);
for even regarding future objects, one may give rise to an evil mind.
One must universally and collectively form the intention to abandon all [unwholesome states] before one can generate the precepts.
Furthermore, if the precepts were not generated regarding the past and future,
the precepts of the Buddhas of the three periods of time would not be equal.
Because the precept-qualities of all Buddhas are equal, they give rise to the precepts throughout the three periods of time. Question:
Precepts prevent what has not yet become non-virtuous.
[Objection: Since the Vinaya has already been established, why can it be said that [the precepts] arise by taking the objects of the three periods of time as their conditions?
Furthermore, would this not contradict the prevention of transgressions throughout the three periods of time? [Answer: No.
Although the object is past, it is not the case that it is "not non-past," and so forth.
For this reason, one must still guard against the fault of [the precept] not yet having arisen;
therefore, this is necessary. Fourth, the extent of the arising of the precepts.
Although the various precepts are numerous, they do not exceed two kinds:
namely, manifest action (vijñapti) and non-manifest action (avijñapti). Once the manifest action has ceased, only non-manifest action remains.
The single continuity of form;
this unmanifest precept (avijñapti-śīla) possesses many categories,
for the evils it prevents are immeasurable.
Precepts are indeed one;
thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"One generates the restraint (*saṃvara*) toward all sentient beings and non-sentient things."
Regarding the phrase "among the number of sentient beings":
this includes all from the highest, the Non-percipient [Heaven], down to the lowest, the Avīci [Hell],
including those who may be killed, those who may be deceived, and those who may not be deceived, and so forth.
From each and every sentient being up to the Tathāgata,
in terms of their fundamental nature, there are no more than seven evils of body and speech,
due to three causes and conditions.
First, seven arise from greed;
second, seven arise from hatred; third, seven arise from delusion.
Thus, there are twenty-one evils in total.
Regarding the prevention of these unwholesome states at the time of receiving the precepts,
it is said that from each of the three wholesome roots— non-attachment and so forth— one attains seven branches of body and speech;
thus, there are twenty-one kinds of virtuous precepts in total.
Even down to every single sentient being throughout the trichiliocosm, it is likewise for all.
If one attains the twelve kinds of precepts through the ten or five precepts,
then the mind will predominantly maintain the two treatises, such that the precepts toward all sentient beings at all times are never interrupted.
Alternatively, because there are twenty-one types,
the Sūtra states:
"Sentient beings are boundless, and the precepts are likewise boundless."
If it is not among the category of sentient beings—
ranging from grasses and trees, seeds, the great earth, non-dharmic clothing and food, and so forth, down to each and every place of transgression— at the time one originally received the precepts.
