The Precept on the Monthly Expectation of Robes (Cīvara-āśā-pratimokṣa), Part Three: I. The Intent of the Regulation.
Robes serve as requisites for the body and are used according to the seasons;
although one may already possess robes, they may become old, tattered, and worn out.
I have merely been able to maintain them through my acceptance of them, but they were not fit for wear.
Now that I have obtained some small amount of wealth, I wish to make three robes;
however, what I have acquired is insufficient to exchange for the old ones and complete a full set.
Therefore, the Noble One opened [this precept].
Because keeping an extra robe beyond one month involves greed and violates the teaching, thereby obstructing the Path, it was established as an offense of falling (pāyattika).
Second, the explanation of the name may be understood [as follows]. Third, there are six specific conditions.
First, if it is a new garment that is currently fit for use,
other wealth is not permitted [to be used],
because the rule applies specifically to garments.
Because of the first condition, the three robes are ruined.
Since the robes must be worn out to obtain wealth,
even if one has enough, one does not accept them, as this would constitute a transgression.
Regarding the second condition, it is insufficient to obtain only a small amount of wealth;
if one does not intend to make the three robes, one merely commits an offense against the first precept, for which there is no exemption.

Regarding the statement "the first month requires the third [robe] for the purpose of providing a substitute for the three robes": this refers to the case where one has not performed the *prasādhana* (purification/dedication) of the four [robes], yet proceeds to make them into the three robes.
Fifth, there is no underlying cause;
sixth, one commits an offense upon exceeding the limit. This precept is explained by analogy through its deficient conditions:
the cause of this precept concerns a bhikṣu who possesses only three robes, for whom a one-month period is permitted as the limit.
If one possesses an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), it may be immediately declared pure (*śuddha-vyavahāra*);
this precept is not required in that case.

If a bhikṣu has finished his robes and the *kāṭhina* robe-season has ended, and he obtains an out-of-season robe (*akāla-cīvara*) which he needs, he may accept it. Having accepted it, he must quickly have it made into a robe. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, he may keep it for one month in order to complete it. If he keeps it beyond that, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. This precept concerning completion originally consists of six phrases.
1. The offender. 2. The exclusion of the occasion for non-offense and the duration of the offense.
3. The types of robes obtained by the bhikṣu and others.
Fourth, once accepted, if one quickly sets foot [upon it], it shall not be opened.
Fifth, if it is insufficient, even though it is insufficient, it shall remain open for a full month.
Sixth, if it exceeds [the limit] and one subsequently sets foot [upon it], one incurs an offense according to the violation.
The following is a detailed explanation: "If a bhikṣu" has the meaning as explained above.
"The robes have been finished and the kaṭhina privileges have been relinquished" means:
It is an offense of long duration once dawn has broken.
If it is within one month after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony,
or during the five months [of the rainy season], these are times when there is no offense.
Regarding the phrase "obtaining out-of-season robes," this clarifies the category of robes obtained.
As for the term "out-of-season":
This refers to exceeding the time limits of one month or five months.
Regarding the statement in the fourth clause that "having received [the precepts], they are quickly established," this clarifies the violation of the time limit.
If one’s robes are sufficient within ten days, one should cut them into pieces,
perform the ritual of purification (śuddhi), and accept them for use.
If not, this continues until the eleventh day.
Regardless of the quantity of robes, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The fifth phrase states that if they are insufficient, one may keep them for one month in order to fulfill the requirement;
this clarifies the second offense.
If the robes are insufficient for a single set, one should prepare them by washing,
dyeing, and performing the ritual purification (*kappiya*) by the eleventh day and then formally accept them.
If one fears they will not be finished, one may perform the "coarse" practice (*lūkha-cariyā*) alongside the completion of the work and then accept them.
If one subsequently cuts them more finely, one avoids the offense of exceeding the prescribed length;
therefore, for those who violate this rule by the twelfth day,
an offense is incurred regardless of the number of robes.
This continues in the same manner up to the twenty-ninth day. If,
by the thirtieth day, it is either sufficient or insufficient—
whether the robes are identical or not identical.
On that very day, one should cut, dye, and wear [the robes].
Fearing that they might not be properly prepared, others may assist so as to avoid transgressing the precept.
There are three exceptions to this rule.
From the tenth day onwards, as long as the conditions for the *kaṭhina* robe remain as they were at the beginning and one has not committed any offense,
then from the eleventh day until the twenty-ninth day, on whichever day the full measure [of robes] is obtained,
one must perform the *śuddhi-vyavahāra* (the ritual of purification) on that very day. Third.
By the thirtieth day, whether the number is sufficient or insufficient,
whether it is the same or different,
one must not grant permission in any case.
The sixth phrase states that if one keeps [the robe] beyond [the permitted time], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This is an offense of transgression against a rule.
Within these offenses, there are four types.
First, relinquish the robe that was transgressed;
second, repent for the offense committed;
third, return to one's original robe.
Fourth, the offense of non-returning.
Regarding the meaning of "not committing an offense," it is as explained in the section on the allowance for extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*).
The fourth precept concerning taking a robe that does not belong to a *bhikṣuṇī*. First, the intent of the regulation.
There are three kinds of faults.
First, when one generally shows respect for inferiors and reverently honors superiors with sincere devotion,
one thinks of relinquishing all one's wealth and possessions as offerings.
It is permitted for one who is not a relative to receive [offerings] from a large assembly of monks without deliberation;
having found such an opportunity, they accept them until the other's wealth is exhausted.
Second, there are those with male and female forms who are distinct.
In principle, there is no escaping these three [transgressions].
Once one has engaged with wealth and property, thoughts of passion arise;
when intimacy is established through such matters, defilement occurs, and the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) is ruined.
When facing perilous matters, one must be extremely cautious;
such conduct invites worldly censure and leads to slander, making it difficult to distinguish one's integrity from corruption.
None are able to extricate themselves from these various transgressions.
For this reason, the Sage established [the precepts]. Second, the explanation of the names may be understood [as follows]. Third, there are five distinct conditions:
first, it concerns bhikṣuṇīs, excluding the two lower assemblies.
According to the *Ji* (the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*), there is no offense regarding the robes of the two assemblies [monks and nuns].
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there is an offense when giving to a nun.
Regarding the two cases of non-relatives, there is no offense provided that one removes the status of being a relative.
Third, it must be of the proper measure and consist of the five robes;
according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the recipient must be one who wears robes of the proper measure for it to be auspicious.
Fourth, it must be given with a sincere heart.
That is to say, it is not an offense to beg for and trade [the items].
However, once one has accepted them and they have come under one's own possession, it is an offense. These four conditions are explained by analogy.
The following section clearly explains the core precept (śīla-mūla).
This precept was established by the Buddha because a bhikṣu who was begging for alms received a costly saṃghāṭī robe from the nun Utpalavarṇā.
Thus, the Buddha promulgated this rule.
If a bhikṣu receives clothing from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and trades it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. This full precept text consists of five phrases.
First, the offender;
second, a nun who is not a relative;
third, the taking of the robe.
Fourth, excluding trade;
fifth, the formal conclusion of the offense.
Below, these are explained in detail.
Regarding the term "if a bhikṣu":
the meaning is as explained above. Regarding "not within a village": [the meaning is as explained above].
Those who are not one's parents or relatives up to the seventh generation are not kin;
conversely, those above this level are kin.
The Treatise says:
Regarding those called "relatives":
they are the blood relations of seven generations, including one's parents.
The *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra* clarifies four kinds of relatives.
1. Father; 2. Parents; 3. Mother and father.
The four mothers and the mother of one's mother—
from these four types of *kappiya-kārī* nuns, taking [an article] is not an offense.
As for what is called "taking clothing":
There are ten kinds of robes.
As explained above in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-śāstra*, if a bhikṣu takes even a single robe belonging to a bhikṣuṇī,
many people commit an offense.
A bhikṣu took a robe from a bhikṣuṇī; because he permitted her [to do so], she committed many offenses.
Therefore, in the Vinaya, the Buddha rebuked the bhikṣuṇī, saying:
Even when a woman wears the finest garments,
she is still unable to inspire a heart of reverence in others,
let alone when she wears tattered and worn-out clothes.
Since it is permitted to keep the five robes at one's discretion,
we know that robes are fundamentally for the support of the body.
To now give them away to others would result in the offense of being without clothing and the violation of the precepts.
If a gift does not accord with the Dharma, it should not be accepted.
However, if one gives freely anything other than the five robes, it may be accepted.
When the Sangha receives a gift from a nun, they should examine and question the donor.
If one knows that the five robes are not complete, one must not accept [the precepts].
If the five robes are complete, one may accept them without fault.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if there was a prior invitation...
If it is given because one is staying in a separate room,
or if it is given for the purpose of preaching the Dharma, there is no offense. According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*,
if one gives as a spontaneous act of charity without the intention of seeking [something in return], there is no offense.
Knowing that the other possesses superior qualities, one does not commit an offense. Question:
Why is it that a bhikṣuṇī who takes a robe belonging to the *saṃgha* incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (light offense)? Answer:
Because the principle is that the Great Saṃgha is superior and venerable to the bhikṣuṇīs.
Because the *kṣudraka* (minor) offenses are not counted [among the formal categories], one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Question:
If that is so, when a monk gives a robe to a nun, it should be a light offense; why then is it a *pāyattika*? Answer:
When a monk gives a robe to a nun, it is prohibited because it falls within the scope of censure and transgression; since the underlying fault (*ādīnava*) is profound, it constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the phrase "except for trade," the Vinaya states:
"The two divisions of the Saṃgha shall divide the robes they have obtained equally."
If one obtains an extra robe by mistake, the Buddha permits its exchange with another.
Regarding the term "exchange" (trading): it refers to...
This refers to trading robes for what is not a robe,
or even trading a single medicinal pill for a robe.
What is called a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* is the fifth formulation of an offense.
Among these, there are four points:
first, one must relinquish the robe;
second, one should perform repentance.
Third, the recipient returns it;
fourth, the giver incurs an offense. There is no offense in the following cases: [list follows].
If one takes it from a relative,
or obtains it through trade,
or takes it for the sake of the Saṃgha or a Buddhist stūpa, there is no offense.
The Fifth Precept: Regarding the Nun’s Washing of Old Clothes. First, the Intent of the Prohibition:
It is the natural order for those of superior rank to have subordinates perform services for them;
however, it is difficult when subordinates repeatedly become indolent and fail to show respect, thereby suppressing their superiors.
Failing to deliberate upon whether resources are available or not leads to causing distress;
neglecting one's duties and damaging one's station results in neither lightness of heart nor freedom from the affliction of defilement;
and when one’s conduct incurs worldly censure, it brings about slander.
Purity and defilement are difficult to distinguish;
one does not know how to extricate oneself from them to benefit others.
For this reason, the Sage established the following inquiry. Question:
Why are washing, dyeing, beating, and so forth subject to regulation? Answer:
First, because the location for nuns is the same;
second, because both cases involve used clothing.

Third, the conditions for the offense: the three factors of having three robes, possessing one robe, and being caused by [the robe] lead to the transgression. If it becomes soiled, it must be washed; if it loses its color, it must be dyed;
if it is stretched out, it becomes stained. Second, the explanation of the name can be understood accordingly. Third, the complete conditions: the general conditions are as stated above.
There are six distinct conditions:
first, she is a bhikṣuṇī;
second, she is not a relative.
Third, it is old clothing.
Fourth, one causes it to be washed, dyed, or beaten.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, if one causes a letter to be written, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are only four cases:
when one washes for oneself and for another, when one causes another to wash for oneself and for another—these two pairs—and when both [wash] together; in all these instances, one commits an offense.
However, in the Vinaya, exceptions are made for these five cases due to the absence of specific causes or conditions.
If one washes, dyes, or beats [a robe] because it is soiled,
or if one borrows another's robe to wash, dye, or beat it, there is no offense.
Apart from such circumstances as these, [there is an offense].
If one has washed, dyed, or beaten [the robe] six times, it constitutes an offense immediately. The four missing conditions are explained by analogy.
Below is the actual core of the precept (*śīla-sūtra*).
This precept originated because Kāḷudāyin sent the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā for a *antarvāsaka* robe from the assembly.
Therefore, the Buddha established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or beat an old garment, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. This complete text consists of five phrases.
1. A single person;
2. a nun who is not a relative;
3. old clothes that have been washed.
Fourth, washing, dyeing, and beating;
fifth, the formal determination of the offense.
Regarding the term "bhikṣu":
As stated above.
Regarding those who are not relatives,
it is also as stated above.
Regarding "worn clothing":
it refers to anything that has been worn on the body at least once.
"Clothing" refers to the ten types of robes.
If new clothes are washed, it brings good fortune.
As for the statements "if dyed" or "if beaten," these refer to the work to be performed.
Regarding the term "niḥsargika-pāyattika":
this refers to an offense.
If one causes a nun's robe to be washed, dyed, or beaten [to soften it], one incurs three pāyattikas.
If one performs two [actions], one incurs two *pāyattikas*;
if one performs one [action], one incurs one *pāyattika*.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
Causing a female renunciant who is one’s wife to wash or dye [the robes] also constitutes an offense.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if one instructs a nun who is not a relative to wash [the robes], yet it is a relative nun who actually washes them,
there are five permutations formed by such mutual actions.

In all cases, one falls into an offense. If one washes or dyes a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), one also commits a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one commits such an offense, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a monk gives a robe to a nun to wash, he commits a minor offense (duṣkṛta).
If, after it has been washed, the monk says it is not yet purified and has the nun wash it again, the nun commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa-duṣkṛta; thus she incurs two offenses.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes [a robe] to be washed, dyed, or beaten, and she herself does not wash it, dye it, or beat it, she incurs three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Other cases where one acts on behalf of another or where duties are shifted may be understood by analogy with this. Question:
Question: Why can the two lower assemblies attain auspiciousness? Answer:
It is because they do not hold their disciples in high regard and thus treat them lightly;
and because even those who do not possess the full precepts do not abandon correct cultivation, and thus [the assembly] treats them lightly.
If one relies on the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, [the offense] for both [a monk and a nun] is the same: a *pāyattika*. Question:
Why is a new robe considered light? Answer:
Because a new robe is rarely washed and lacks the conditions for wear and tear, it incurs only a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
Regarding those who do not commit an offense,
the Vinaya states:
"If it is for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha— such as having them wash or dye [robes]— there is no fault."

The Sixth Precept: Begging for Robes from a Layperson Who Is Not a Relative. Generally, those who have left the household life should practice contentment and ensure that their three robes are complete, so as not to be separated from them while traveling on long journeys.
To beg extensively for alms increases greed and distresses others,
inviting the reproach and faults of the world.
The damage is not slight;
therefore, the Sage established this rule.
There are six distinct conditions.
1. Being fully provided with the three robes;
2. Having no [valid] reason;
3. [The donor being] a householder who is not a relative.
Fourth, one requests a robe of the proper measure for oneself;
fifth, the other person gives it;
sixth, upon receiving and taking possession of it, one commits an offense. This is understood by analogy through the deficiency of conditions.
The following section clearly elucidates the core of the precept (*śīla-sūtra*).
This precept was established because the householder Upananda forcibly solicited robes from laypeople,
which led others to criticize and disparage him.

To enter [the path] for one's own benefit is itself skillful means and is blameless.
One should understand the categories of those that are both blameworthy and blameless.
As for not committing an offense:
The Vinaya states:
"It is permitted for the five classes of renunciants to engage in mutual trade,
provided they examine and determine [the value] for themselves."
One should not engage in mutual bargaining or haggling over prices as is the custom in the marketplace.
One must not trade with others personally; rather, one should have a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) conduct the trade.
If one repents after having heard [the rule],
or if one exchanges it for ghee, there is no offense,
as this is permitted for the purpose of providing offerings for lamps.
The Twenty-first Precept: Regarding the Keeping of an Extra Alms Bowl Beyond the Limit. The intention behind this regulation is as follows:
the alms bowl is a vessel for receiving offerings;
it is sufficient for the sustenance of the body.
Now, excessive hoarding increases greed, obstructs the Path,
and invites worldly reproach and disgrace.
Repeated damage and loss are not insignificant;
therefore, the Sage established these regulations.
Nevertheless, as the conditions of material things are ever-changing, there may be occasions where one's basic necessities for sustaining life are lost or stolen.
Necessary affairs must not be neglected.
If one does not accept them at the time they are offered,
it will be difficult to obtain them later.
Therefore, the ten-day period for declaring purity (*śuddhi*) was established;

yet, if one keeps [the items] beyond that limit, it constitutes a transgression. According to the Holy Teaching, a transgression results in the formal commission of an offense (*āpatti*). To explain the terminology:
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there is a case where a bhikṣu obtained an alms-bowl.
Because the Buddha did not permit the keeping of extra bowls, he gave it to another;
subsequently, his own bowl broke.
The Buddha asked how long after [the full moon] it would be broken.
He replied, "Ten days.
Consequently, he permitted a ten-day period.

Because the fourfold division [of the *Prātimokṣa*] was subsequently expanded by ten days at the request [of the Buddha], it is called the precept against keeping an almsbowl for more than ten days. There are five distinct aspects to this:
first, there is the bowl that one already possesses and maintains.
Second, obtaining a bowl;
third, a bowl that is in accordance with the Dharma is not a transgression—
meaning it possesses the three "in accordance with" criteria.
Fourth, impure giving.
Fifth, the offense of transgressing the ten-day limit due to a deficiency in the requisite conditions;
these may be understood through the preceding explanations.
The following clearly explains the root of the precept.
This precept arose because the group of six bhikṣus sought many fine alms bowls,
which led householders to criticize and disparage them.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression, and the Buddha then established the precept:

"If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl without having performed the formal act of dedication (*apariśuddha-dāna*), and it exceeds ten days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. This full text of the precept consists of four phrases.
First, the offender;
second, the extra bowl he possesses;
third, the allowance for keeping it for ten days.
The fourth [point] concerns the formal offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
The first phrase is self-evident.
As for the term "extra bowl" (*atireka-pātra*):
The Vinaya states:
"There are six kinds of bowls:
the iron bowl, the black bowl, the bowl from the country of Kṛṣṇasoma, the bowl from the country of Ujjala, and the bowl from the country of Ugasa."
There are two essentials:
first, an iron bowl;
second, an earthenware bowl.
Regarding these two types of bowls,
they must possess three qualities to be fit for formal acceptance and use.
First, as for the bowl, it may be made only of clay or iron;
second, as for its capacity, the large one is three sheng and the small one is one and a half sheng.
Third is the theory that form is seen as it appears.
An iron almsbowl undergoes five fumigations;
an ordinary bowl undergoes three fumigations.
Only above is this the full extent of form (*rūpa*).
These three directions can be described as pure.
As for what is called "impure giving":
These are the conditions for an offense.
There are two kinds of offenses:
first, transgressions.
The second is the offense through defilement (*sāpattika*).
This is presented through eight relative categories;
it is no different from the rules regarding extra robes (*atirekacīvara*).
The ten days of fasting are the permitted limit;
therefore, the Vinaya says:
Ānanda obtained the bowl and wished to offer it to Kāśyapa; however,
because he used it daily, he would have to return it within ten days,
fearing that he might incur the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
He reported the matter to the Buddha,
who permitted [the keeping of the robe] for up to ten days.
Regarding what was called "exceeding [the limit]," it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This is the section on the characteristics of offenses resulting from transgressing time limits.
The allowance is as in the case of the precept on extra robes.
The twenty-second precept: Begging for a Bowl. The intention behind the regulation is as follows:
However, his alms bowl has fewer than five patches and does not leak;
it is fit for use in supporting the body.
Yet now, he wanders everywhere seeking [food] from those who are not relatives.
Prolonged greed obstructs the Path and disturbs the donor;
this is contrary to principle and improper.
Therefore, one must observe the noble prohibitions. There are six specific conditions:
first, one must already possess a bowl that has been formally accepted;
second, it must have fewer than five patches and not leak.
Third, begging from those who are not relatives;
fourth, for one's own sake;
fifth, begging for a bowl that is in accordance with the Dharma.
The sixth [offense] is committed upon receiving [the object].
Below this, the actual precept text (*śikṣāpada*) is clearly explained.
This precept arose because Ba-nan-da’s bowl was broken.
Consequently, he begged for many bowls from many householders and was thus subjected to criticism and reproach.
The bhikṣus reported this transgression.
The Buddha, because of this, established the precept:

"If a bhikṣu possesses a bowl that has fewer than five mends and is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it; the Saṃgha shall take the lowest-ranking bowl from among those in circulation and give it to him to keep until it breaks. This is the proper procedure. This fundamental rule of the precept consists of two sections.
The preceding section clarified the rules regarding the begging for a bowl and the offenses involved;
this section clarifies the proper procedure for returning it.
The first part, the root text of the precept, consists of three sections.
1. The first offender;
2. An old bowl that has not yet reached its full [allowable] limit;
3. Seeking another [bowl] while still bound by the offense.
The first passage is clear.
Regarding the second passage, which states that "the bowl has fewer than five patches and does not leak," the Vinaya says:
"A space of two finger-breadths apart is one stitch.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" is the third formula for the offense.
From the passage beginning with "That bhikṣu... down to this point is the section on the timing;
it clarifies the rules for returning after having relinquished [the robes]. Within this, there are two parts.
The first point, "one should go before the Saṃgha," clarifies the relinquishing of the bowl;
the second point, "having passed it on in succession," and those that follow, constitute a single sentence.
General Discussion on the Text for Returning the Alms Bowl:

Regarding the phrase "this is the proper time," it refers to the period when one uses the old bowl to hold [food] while holding the new one, until the old one breaks and becomes fit to be held; this applies to the four sections below concerning the returning of the bowl.
This is explained in detail as set forth in the Vinaya:
first, the method for relinquishing the bowl;
second, the ritual for repentance.
Third, returning the bowl;
fourth, not returning it constitutes an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).
There are four ways in which one initially relinquishes the bowl.
First, carrying the alms bowl to the Sangha;
second, entering the boundary;
third, the deportment.
Fourth is the formula for relinquishing [the bowl].
Second, the confession of offenses is as explained above.
Third, the text for returning the bowl also consists of four parts.
1. If a person of high status seizes and retains [the bowl], it should be returned;
the bowl should be given to a junior monk. 2. The Saṃgha should act so as to give it themselves to a junior monk, having him hold it.
3. The offending bhikṣu should be penalized by being made to hold a new bowl while using the old one.
Fourth, because it must be protected against the fear of being damaged, a new one is used.

Therefore, according to the Vinaya, when a monk gives a lower bowl, he should grant it to that person with a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one announcement), and [the recipient] should protect it.
One must not place it where tiles or stones might fall upon it, nor lean it against a staff or under a blade.
One must not hang objects over the middle of a path, nor upon stones, fruit trees, or uneven ground.
One must not hold two bowls with a single hand;
however, it is permissible to hold two bowls with one hand provided that the fingers are separated by the space between them.
One must not open the door except when necessary for the sake of practice;
furthermore, one should not intentionally damage it or cause it to be lost.
It is not for use as an almsbowl.
These four passages all refer to taking that fine bowl from him;
it is to be passed through the Saṃgha in order until the lowest, most inferior bowl among the assembly is taken and given to him to carry.
Because it serves to quell the fault of greed.
The fourth section, "Returning the Bowl," has two parts:
returning it due to having a valid reason.
If the *karman* (formal act) has been performed overnight without a formal invitation, one may return.
According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, if the bowl is expensive,
one should take the value of ten bowls.
Nine bowls are kept in the eight clean kitchens;
one bowl’s worth is returned directly to the owner.
If one obtains the value of two bowls by begging, [the same applies].
One bowl shall enter the Sangha;
one bowl shall be returned to its owner.
In this manner, according to how much or how little is obtained, they are limited to returning exactly that amount to the owner.
The others entered the monastic kitchen directly.
Regarding the fourth case of one who incurs an offense by not returning,
the Vinaya states:
If one has discarded a bowl among the Saṃgha and does not return it, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one instructs another not to return it, that too is a *duṣkṛta*.
Among those who do not commit an offense: [none].
The Vinaya states:
"If one has five patches and yet seeks new ones, or if one demands new ones from [the Sangha] after [the old ones] have been obtained."
One may seek it from those who have left the household life;
or if one obtains it without seeking for oneself or others,
or if one obtains it through successive acts of giving.
If one purchases livestock with its own price, there is no offense in any case.
The twenty-third precept:
regarding the rule against begging for thread and having a non-relative weave it. The intention behind the regulation is as follows:
"Although one's body can be sustained by possessing the three robes in full,
you have now personally begged for thread and relied upon your influence and status to compel a weaver to weave these three robes for you."
Long harboring greed and excessive desire,
he caused distress to the weaver and,
in turn, reviled and slandered him.
Therefore, the Noble One established four distinct conditions:
first, personally soliciting thread;
second, having a lay weaver who is not a relative weave it.
Third, she sends away the weaver by means of intimidation and does not pay the price;
fourth, the offense is committed once it is completed.
Below this, the core of the precept (śikṣāpada) is correctly explained.
This rule of the *Prātimokṣa* originated from the transgression of Upananda; therefore, the Buddha established this precept:
"If a bhikṣu himself solicits thread and has a non-relative weave it into a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. This complete formulation of the rule consists of four phrases.
First, one commits the offense oneself;
second, one must personally beg for thread—since begging from a layperson constitutes a subsequent offense—one must therefore beg for it oneself.
If one does not beg for the thread oneself, the offense should be considered light.
If one compels a weaver by force to work,
there is no offense if it is obtained through reasoned persuasion;
likewise, there is no transgression if payment is given.
There are four offenses involving formal acts (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). The detailed explanation of the two preceding phrases [of the verse] can be understood from above.
As for the statement, "having a weaver who is not a relative weave a robe":
The *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there are three cases regarding a weaver who is not a relative.

This precept specifically clarifies that one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) when directly causing harm to a weaver who is not a relative; begging for thread from such a person constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*).
Regarding the weaver being either a relative or a non-relative, there are three cases.
When the weaver is a relative from one's own village, there are two cases, with one matter omitted.
In the third case, where both are relatives, there is no offense.
Therefore, there are only eight cases: if one merely damages the weaver, one commits a *thullaccaya*;
if one damages both the weaver and the owner of the yarn, one commits a *pācittiya* for each instance.
Because it comprehensively includes both heavy and light offenses, it simply states "one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. This constitutes the fourth section:
the demarcation of the determination of offenses.
The procedure for relinquishing and confessing [the offense] is explained extensively in the Vinaya.
Regarding non-offenses:
The Vinaya states:
"If both [the donor and the recipient] are relatives,
and one weaves for oneself a bowl-bag, a leather-shoe bag, a needle-case, a meditation belt, a waistband, a cap, a tunic, a hair-puller, a hot-towel, or a lining for leather shoes or a towel."
In all cases, there is no offense.
The twenty-fourth precept: Exhorting and praising a weaver to increase the weaving of robes.
The intent of the regulation is that a layperson of sincere faith, with an open mind, provided thread to a bhikṣu.
Therefore, when weaving the three robes,
one should receive them in accordance with the donor's intention;
thus, within oneself, there shall be a sense of integrity and moderation.
Previously she did not trouble her master;
now she even encourages and praises the weaver,
personally providing him with the payment.
To harm another is to ruin one's own mental conduct;
it benefits neither oneself nor others. Therefore, the Noble One established six distinct conditions.
First, a layperson personally prepares the thread and dispatches a weaver to weave it;
second, there is a finite expectation;
third, one knows it is finite.
Fourth, encouraging the weaving by offering payment;
fifth, increasing the amount of thread for him;
sixth, accepting it, which constitutes an offense.
Below, the core of the precept (śikṣāpada) is formally explained.
This precept originated because of Upananda,
who went to a layperson’s house to select threads and give them to a weaver.
Furthermore, they agreed to pay the price;
the householder criticized and disparaged them,
and the bhikṣus reported the transgression.
The Buddha then established this precept:

"If a bhikṣu, when a householder or a householder’s wife has sent a weaver to weave a robe for a bhikṣu, goes to the weaver’s place before having received a formal invitation and says: 'Weave this robe for me; weave it very well, making it wide, large, and firm, and I shall give you a small amount of price,' and if that bhikṣu gives the price of the robe—even if it is worth only a single meal—and obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. This precept has three [distinctions]."
First, the brief;
second, the expansion;
third, the fulfillment.
The four factors for fulfillment:
first, the offender;
second, the owner of the yarn who dispatches [the weaver] to weave the three robes.
3. That bhikṣu [down to] even encouraging a weaver to hire laborers by paying their wages himself;
4. If he obtains [the robe], down to the conclusion of the offense.
The first two phrases can be understood.
The statement, "If a bhikṣu has not previously accepted an invitation for a *pravāraṇā*," is the opening text.
The Vinaya says:
The Buddha did not permit [monks] to go to the house where robes were being made.
Later, there was a layperson who invited a bhikṣu and offered him a robe.
The bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to go.
Consequently, the Buddha permitted them to go as they pleased,
provided they took those who were of few desires, contented, and sought what was inferior.
The meaning of the remaining phrases is clear and may be understood. Question:
What is the difference between this and the preceding "weaving of the precepts"? Answer:
There are four differences.
First, the former [offense] harms the weaver but does not harm the owner of the thread,
because it was obtained through begging.
In this case, the harm falls upon the owner of the yarn, not upon the weaver.
Regarding the second [offense], under the previous precept, one commits an offense by harming the weaver through the failure to pay the wage;
in this case, one commits an offense because the owner of the yarn fails to pay the wage.
Third, it is an offense when committed by one who is not a relative;
if one is a relative, there is no offense. This refers to offenses committed by both relatives and non-relatives.
Regarding the four [offenses]: one commits an offense immediately upon weaving the threads oneself;
this [offense] occurs only when one receives threads belonging to another.
As the Vinaya states:
There is no offense if one has previously accepted an invitation; if one goes seeking with contentment and without excessive seeking;
or if one requests from relatives.
One solicits from those who have left the household life;
or one solicits for another;
or another solicits on one's behalf.
Or, if one obtains [an item] without seeking it, there is no offense in any case.
The twenty-fifth precept concerning the taking of a bhikṣu’s robe: the intent of the regulation is as follows.
Previously, he gave me a robe with the intention that we might travel together;
since he is unwilling to go,
it is only right that I should act with conciliation.
Yet, seeking [what is owed] is inherently without fault;
it is when one forcibly seizes it with a mind of anger that mutual affliction occurs.
This is particularly inappropriate;
therefore, a sacred regulation is required.
There are five distinct conditions [for this].
First, because the bhikṣu Jien (Jiṇa) śrāmaṇera did not commit any improper acts;
second, because he had previously given him a robe with the intention that they would travel together;
and third, because giving it to one person indeterminate[ly] and taking it back from another indeterminate[ly] would have caused great distress.
Of the four propositions, in the first two, the initial acceptance and the act itself are both determinate;
in the second, the determination is present while the acceptance is indeterminate.
To seize by force constitutes a grave offense.
If one receives [the object] together with the intention [to steal], it is indeterminate;
if one seizes it through strong anger, it is a transgression;
and if one acquires an object and it comes under one's own possession, one commits an offense.
Below, the core precept (śīla-mūla) is correctly elucidated.
This precept was established by the Buddha because Nanda committed a transgression.

If a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger, either takes it back himself or instructs another to take it back, saying, "Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you," he must return the robe. If he takes it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. This complete original text consists of three phrases.
First, the offender;
second, the prior giving of the robe;
third, the subsequent taking back with the intent to do so, which constitutes the offense.
The first sentence is easily understood.
Regarding the second sentence: because he originally intended to practice together with him, he gave him the robe;
later, when the other refused, he consequently seized it by force.
Therefore it is said: "First, give the robe to the bhikṣu.
Regarding the third phrase, "taking back," the Vinaya states:
If one seizes it oneself out of anger or instructs another to seize it and then conceals it, one commits an offense;
that is, seizing it while it is present before one's eyes.
If one seizes it but does not conceal it, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If the matter has not yet been divided and the formal rule has not yet been established, one incurs an offense upon the initial transgression.
If [the object] is placed upon a tree, a yoke, a bed, or any other such place,
one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for the act of separation from that place.
Therefore, the Prātimokṣa states:
"To take a robe constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The procedure for relinquishing and confessing this offense is as clarified in the Vinaya.
Regarding those who do not commit an offense,
the Vinaya states:
"One does not speak out of anger."
"I regret not having given it;
return my robe to me.
If that person feels remorse, they may immediately return the robe.
If another person says,
"This bhikṣu wishes to repent and return the robe to you," or "He is borrowing this robe from you to wear."
There is no offense in taking back [an object] without justification if one fears it will be lost or destroyed,
or if the person has broken their precepts, their views, or their deportment.
If one has been suspended and their body must be cremated, it should be cremated. If,
for the sake of this matter, there is a threat to life or a danger involving non-Brahmins,
no one shall seize or conceal the items that have been set aside.
In all these cases, there is no offense.
The twenty-sixth precept: Regarding the rule against keeping medicine for more than seven days. First, the intent behind its establishment:
Ordinary people take the four great elements as their vehicle and are driven by anxiety.
At the transition between the end of autumn and the beginning of winter, the four great elements contend and undergo transformation, whereby various illnesses immediately arise.
Once such afflictions exist, they obstruct and cause the abandonment of the cultivation of the Path.
The Great Sage, out of compassion,
has skillfully permitted the keeping [of these items] so that one may take various medicines to treat the suffering of illness.
This is intended to allow them to settle their bodies and advance in their spiritual practice,
as permitted by the Sage.
To stockpile a wide variety of medicines is to increase greed and ruin one's practice;
it violates the teachings and invites reproach and transgression.
Because it is not to be treated lightly, this is established as a *pāyattika* offense. Second, regarding the explanation of the name:
to store and use for one's own benefit is termed "possessing" (*parikkhāra*).
To treat illness is termed "medicine" (*bhesajja*); when it exceeds its designated period, it is termed "seven-day transgression."
Therefore it is said: "The precept against storing medicine for more than seven days. Regarding the three conditions, the general conditions are as stated above.
There are four specific conditions:
first, it must be a seven-day medicine.
Second, there is the acceptance through both hands and mouth.
Third, not declaring it as pure.
Fourth, keeping it beyond seven days constitutes an offense. These four absences of conditions should be understood by analogy.
Below, the core precept (śīla-mūla) is correctly elucidated.
This precept was established by the Buddha because a transgression arose involving a disciple of Pindola Bharadvāja.

If a bhikṣu, being ill, keeps leftover medicinal substances—clarified butter, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock honey—and consumes them for up to seven days; if he consumes them beyond seven days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. This complete precept text consists of five phrases.
First, the person who commits the offense;
second, the circumstances for a sick person to keep medicine;
third, the nature of the medicine kept, such as leftover medicine and so forth.
Fourth, the opening [of the period] lasts for seven days.
Fifth, exceeding the limit constitutes an offense.
Regarding the initial phrase in the subsequent explanation, it may be understood as stated.
Regarding the second phrase, "one who has an illness," the Vinaya states:
"In the autumn months,
wind-disorders (vāta) are stirred up, causing the physical form to become withered and parched."
Furthermore, the arising of malignant sores and the like are the conditions for storing medicine.
The third statement regarding "residual medicine"— namely ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock honey—
refers to the actual substances of the medicine that may be stored.
Regarding the fourth statement, "one may consume [it] for up to seven days," this is the opening limit;
the meaning of its eightfold categories is as explained in the *Dīrghacīvara* (Long-Robe) precept.
Regarding the fifth statement, "if one consumes it beyond seven days, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
This constitutes the offense of exceeding the limit.
The Vinaya states:
"If one obtains medicine on the first day, or even up to the seventh day, and then [retains it] until the eighth day."
When the first day’s medicine exceeds [the limit] and taints the subsequent six days, one commits an offense in proportion to the amount of medicine involved;
therefore, it is said that all constitute *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses. Question:
When the medicine of the subsequent six days is tainted by the offense, does the formal acceptance (*paribhoga*) of that medicine become lost?
Because there are two types of non-understanding,
I shall now first explain the purification through declaration (*śuddhivācanā*) regarding transgressions;
the following six days have likewise not yet been purified through declaration.
Because they belong to the same stage of development,
they serve as the primary objects for the defiled experience of the mouth; thus,
they act as obstacles to previously acquired understanding.
It does not preclude [the use of] long [medicines].
Since the purposes for which they are used differ and the time limit has not yet expired, [they may be kept].
Medicine taken on the first day cannot be stained by subsequent [medicines] and causes all [previous] acceptances to be lost.
Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"On the seventh day, the medicine is given to the bhikṣus as food."
If the possession were to be lost, then past liberation and so forth would arise immediately;
for what purpose, then, would one listen to the teaching on food? Therefore, we know that it is not lost.
If that were so, the remaining five days [of the meal] should be returned to the owner;
as for the food, one should instead use it to anoint the feet and light a lamp. Answer:
In truth, there is no loss of the vow, and both [acts] are minor offenses.
The purpose of storing [medicines] is to remedy mental faults;
therefore, they are not permitted to be consumed if stored for too long.
This is because mental faults are pacified by medicine, whereas that which is impure cannot do so.
Unlike the case of clothing, which serves the purpose of sustaining the body,
[the robe] may be returned to its original owner and subsequently used as clothing once again.
The remaining phrases are to be understood by analogy.
The Vinaya states:
"This medicine should be relinquished to the Saṃgha."
Having finished the self-confession and returned that medicine,
on the seventh day one should give the medicine to a bhikṣu;
he should then consume it.
Medicine kept for more than seven days should have clarified butter smeared on its opening;
honey should be given to the garden keeper;
that which has been kept for less than seven days should be returned through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation).
A bhikṣu shall take [the oil] to anoint his feet and light a lamp.
There is no offense as described above.
The two precepts concerning requesting rain-clothing too early and using it too early constitute the twenty-seventh [section]. These two precepts are established together.
According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there is also a fault in requesting before the [proper time] and a fault in using before the [proper time]; both constitute a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Therefore, it is not permitted to request or use [the robe] before the [proper time]. As for "requesting and using before the [proper time]": [it refers to the following].
However, this rain-clothing is a necessary provision for sustaining the body;
therefore, it was permitted to be sought and used during the designated season.
To seek it out and use it beforehand when the time has not yet arrived is merely an expression of one's own greed and attachment, which violates the holy teachings.
Therefore, the Sage established the rule: there are five reasons for seeking [robes] prior to the [regular] time.
First is the rain-cloak;
second is seeking prior to the [regular] time.
Third, for oneself;
fourth, he gives it;
fifth, upon receiving it, one commits an offense.
Compared to the previous [rule], the specific conditions for this transgression regarding the use of robes consist of four factors:
first, it must be one's own rain-cloak;
second, it must be obtained during a non-seasonal period.
The first offense occurs when one accepts [the robe] before the three prescribed times; the second occurs when one uses it before the four prescribed times.

Regarding the inferiority of one's occupation:
you are a person of arts and crafts.
Regarding the inferiority of one's appearance: [you are so].
"You are one who is blind and sightless.
To say that those who commit transgressions are base means that you yourself are a person who commits transgressions."
Regarding the statement "you are base due to fetters and afflictions," it means that you are one who is driven by many fetters and afflictions.
As for the second matter of reproach, there are three points.
First, direct verbal abuse;
second, metaphorical abuse;
third, abuse by comparison with oneself.
Regarding "verbal abuse," it refers to such things as saying,
"You are born into a family of scavengers," and so forth.
Regarding "abusive speech by means of metaphors," it refers to...
"You resemble those of the scavenger caste and so forth.
As for what you call "insulting by analogy," I am not of the scavenger caste.
Furthermore, I do not trade with those who slaughter oxen, sheep, or people who are lame or crippled.
Moreover, there are three ways of reviling while performing wholesome deeds.
As for reviling in one's face:
"You are one who dwells in an araṇya and practices meditation," and so forth;
the other two cases should be understood by analogy.
Regarding the third phrase, it says "pāyattika."
This is the text concerning the establishment of the offense.
Regarding its gravity, there are two aspects:
first, those who revile a bhikṣu with any of the six kinds of evil speech all incur a *pāyattika* offense.
Second, regarding the three kinds of verbal abuse involving wholesome dharmas, all constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Within the category of verbal abuse involving unwholesome dharmas,
if one abuses a bhikṣu or one's parents, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one reviles one’s preceptor (upādhyāya) or instructor (ācārya), one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if one reviles one’s relatives, close friends, or fellow students, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Vinaya states:
Beyond the aforementioned insults, there is another case where one commits an offense:
namely, when a bhikṣu of low birth lives together with one of high birth and says,
"In this community, there is a bhikṣu of low birth."
Regarding those who do not commit an offense,
the Vinaya states:
"If one speaks for the sake of mutual benefit."
It is spoken for the sake of the Dharma;
it is spoken for the sake of the Vinaya;
it is spoken for the sake of instruction.
It is spoken for the sake of a friend;
or out of joy or laughter, or due to conversation;
subsequently, it may be spoken through a slip of the tongue or by way of incidental contact.
If one speaks erroneously, there is no offense in either case.
The third precept on the prohibition against divisive speech: the regulation of the mind.
Now, those who have left the household life should dwell together with a mind free from discrimination;
yet they instead conspire in secret,
whispering things back and forth between one another.
It causes disputes that did not previously exist among the Saṃgha to arise, and it makes existing disputes impossible to extinguish.
Hearing of such turmoil within the monastic community brings heavy distress to the heart.
Therefore, the Noble One established six distinct conditions:
first, [the offender must be] a virtuous *bhikṣu* of great standing,
excluding other assemblies as well as those who assist in causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
Second, speaking of base and evil matters;
third, transmitting [words] from one person to another;
fourth, forming the intention to cause separation.
The five-character verses are clear and distinct;
the preceding six lines are known by the author.
As the Treatise says:
Causing a schism among the great bhikṣus is a grave offense;
other offenses are lighter.
This is because causing a schism among bhikṣus may result in the formation of separate factions.
The matter of causing a schism in the Saṃgha is grave for this reason;
there are also four cases, which can be understood from what has been said above.
The following clearly elucidates the core precept (*śikṣāpada*).
This precept was established because the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*) spread rumors back and forth among others,
causing strife and contention within the Saṃgha.
Unable to extinguish it,
the bhikṣu reported the transgression.
The Buddha then cited the example of two beasts— a jackal and a wild animal— engaged in a quarrel.
How much more so regarding human beings!
Thus, he established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu speaks with double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika. This complete precept consists of three sentences in its original text.
First, the offender;
second, the double-tongued speech;
third, the formal determination of the offense.
The first phrase is self-evident.
Regarding the second, "double-tongued speech" (slander):
it refers to inciting discord between two parties to cause them to break apart.
Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"To cause strife and confusion among ten members of the assembly applies equally to the five groups of the ordained and likewise to those of the laity."
The three instances of "pāyattika" (offense requiring expiation) constitute the textual formulation of the transgression.
The Vinaya states:
If one causes strife among the bhikṣus, one commits a *thullaccaya*;
the other nine cases are all minor offenses.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
He proclaims unwholesome dharmas, saying: "So-and-so says this;
you are devoid of superior, middling, or inferior dharmas," desiring to cause others to abandon them.
If one either separates from them or does not separate from them, both cases constitute a downfall.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that this is a downfall because it is spoken repeatedly;
furthermore, if one does not transmit the words between the two parties, it constitutes a downfall.
However, regarding the two sides speaking of union or separation, all such instances constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Among those that do not constitute an offense,
the Vinaya states:
If one breaks away from evil associates and wicked companions—
such as preceptors, fellow teachers, relatives, friends, and spiritual mentors—
and acts to the detriment of the Sangha, the stupas, and the temples.
If one intends to act for the sake of what is not beneficial and thus causes such a person to break [their vows],
there is no offense whatsoever.
The Fourth Precept: Sleeping in the Same Room with a Woman. The intention behind this regulation is that the physical forms of men and women are distinct; logically, they should not cohabit.
When their spheres of activity intersect, there is the potential for the arising of defilement and impurity.
Furthermore, it leads to ridicule and disgrace;
one cannot extricate oneself from these afflictions, which are no light matter.
Therefore, the Sage established five distinct conditions.
First, she is a human woman;
second, her physical characteristics are fully formed;
third, they share the same room for lodging.
Fourth, sleeping together.
Fifth, incurring an offense by turning over while lying down with her. Regarding the term "human woman":
[it refers to a female human being].
In the four or five rules concerning the taking of a human female,
one excludes other women and distinguishes her from men and so forth;
it concerns only a human female, regardless of whether she is a monastic or a layperson, a relative or a stranger, or young or old.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that [the prohibition applies] from birth until death, excluding female infants.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the twelve rules apply to women of all three realms of existence.
That is to say, the *Ji* states:
"Mothers, daughters, sisters, those senior or junior, whether monastics or laypeople—all are objects of transgression.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
It is an offense in all cases of staying overnight with women of the three [lower] destinies;
likewise if it be a female camel, horse, ox, or sheep,
whether they be lying down or standing.
If a goose, hawk, peacock, falcon,
or similar bird stands on one leg with its head placed upon the crown of the head, it is called "having committed a transgression while staying overnight.
This applies even if there is a woman in another's house.
Staying overnight with a guest cat also constitutes an offense.
Regarding "staying together with one who knows of the four [conditions]," the offense is incurred simply by knowing that one is staying there.
These two cases differ:
[the offense] must necessarily be committed through a prior agreement.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, if it concerns one's mother, daughter, sister, or other close relatives who are ill...
If one knows that the bedding is not suitable for oneself, there is no offense.
This Vinaya text below permits no offense when one is ill;
in contrast to this illness-based exemption, a formal condition (*pratyaya*) should likewise be established.
Below, the core of the precept (*śīla-sūtra*) is formally elucidated.
This precept originated because Aniruddha, while traveling on a road, stayed overnight at the house of a courtesan and was seduced by her.
The Venerable One ascended into the void;
he felt shame and repented, and through the teaching of the Dharma, he attained the Path.
The bhikṣus reported the transgression, and the Buddha then established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika. This full formulation of the precept consists of four phrases.
First, a male offender;
second, a woman;
third, sleeping in the same room.
There are four cases of offenses.
The first phrase is self-evident.
Regarding the second, which speaks of "giving to a woman":
The Vinaya states:

"If a human woman possesses discernment and her life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not severed, she is called a 'woman'. Regarding the three mentions of the *Śravaṇā* lunar mansion: [it refers to the time when the moon is in conjunction with that mansion].
There are four kinds of rooms. First,
those with enclosures on all four sides and a roof above,
such that they are situated within the same hall.
If there is a partition within it, it is not permissible according to the treatise.
Second, "open at the front with no walls" refers to a long rectangular room where the two ends are enclosed by screens.
Third, although it is covered, it is not all-encompassing;
this is like a single gate atop a courtyard where the roof extends over it but leaves the center open.
Fourth, although it is covered all over, there are openings.
This refers to a structure generally covered and obstructed above, with only a small opening or light-hole.
Regarding the term "lodging" (*sodha*):
this refers to the precept concerning a bhikṣu sharing a lodging with a woman within these four types of rooms.
The woman arrives later;
or the bhikṣu arrives later;
or both arrive at the same time.
If one lies down and turns from side to side, each instance constitutes an offense.
Regarding the four terms "pāyattika": [it refers to] an offense requiring expiation.
This is an offense category.
Within it, there are two [subdivisions].
If one sleeps in the same room as a woman, for every turn of the body, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one sleeps in the same room as a woman, an animal, a human, a eunuch, or a person with dual sexual organs, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu lies down for the entire day while a woman stands, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a woman sits [with a man] in a secluded place, she commits a *pāyattika* offense.

According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if they gather together in the assembly hall within the same enclosure, even if they enter and exit separately, they both commit the offense.
According to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, if one sits through the entire night inside a room, there is no offense.
One must certainly stay together with many others who are knowledgeable and do not sleep.
The *Jì* states:
"If there is a separate room with a partitioned door, there is no offense."
If one is preaching the Dharma throughout the night at a great assembly and, due to wind, rain, cold, or snow in the open air, wishes to enter a room,
one should sit upright with the body straightened.
If one is too old or ill to sit, [one may do otherwise].
When constructing a screen for alms-food, one must not use coarse materials;
it should be as high as the shoulders and armpits,
and from the bottom to the ground, it must not allow even a cat to pass through.
If there is no partition, one may speak with a trustworthy woman, saying:
"You lie down first;
I shall sit."
A bhikṣu wished to sleep.
He said, "Wake me up;
I wish to sleep."
Do not sleep. If you sleep, you will have no meritorious conduct.
According to the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, if one stays overnight with ten women, one incurs ten *pārājika* offenses.
Each successive transgression results in ten *pārājika* offenses.
If one stays in the same room as a woman in a layperson’s house without closing the door, it is a *duṣkṛta*; this is not included among the [offenses] that do not constitute a violation.
The Vinaya states:
"If one was previously unaware that there was a woman in the room, or if it does not constitute the characteristics of a 'room' (a private dwelling), [there is no offense]."
Whether sitting, walking, or ill;
whether thrown down by forceful means, or bound by others.
If one addresses [the Buddha] as "Brahmā" and so forth, there is no offense in either case.
The Fifth Precept: Regarding the prohibition against staying overnight in the same room as one who has not received full ordination beyond the prescribed limit.
The intention behind the regulation is that, in general, the paths of the monastic and the lay diverge, and their dispositions and affairs are contrary to one another.

When first practicing and not yet having closed off the senses, one is often troubled by external distractions; if these are nearby, arrogance arises, which disturbs the Way and causes the abandonment of practice.
Therefore, it is appropriate to stay in a separate location to preserve the Way and increase one's reverence.
Therefore, it must be regulated.
However, those who have left the household life dwell with no fixed mind and travel about;
they seek lodging with others to maintain their physical form and sustain their lives.
Furthermore, since śrāmaṇeras leave the secular world and rely on this [monastic] refuge,
they have no other support and require the company of others; for this reason,
permission is granted for them to remain for a limited period of two nights.
However, prohibition serves to prevent excess, while opening serves to facilitate benefit.
That which is appropriate for the principles of opening and restricting is exactly what ought to be so. There are five distinct conditions that must be complete.
First, regarding the phrase "a man who has not yet received full ordination," women are excluded because the Buddha did not permit staying in the same room as a woman;
since he never even permitted [staying for] two nights,
how could there be the fault of exceeding three?
Therefore, the *Gāthā-śāstra* says:
"Having stayed overnight with a śrāmaṇera for two nights,
one stays overnight with a woman on the third night."
One incurs two *thullaccaya* offenses:
second, the accomplishment of the characteristics of a private chamber;
third, sharing a common chamber.
Fourth, knowing they are in the same room;
fifth, exceeding three nights [of staying together] constitutes an offense of *pāyattika*.
Below this, the actual precept text is clearly elucidated.
This precept text consists of three parts:
first, a brief prohibition;
second, a restatement of that prohibition followed by an allowance for two nights and three nights.
The detailed regulations follow later.
As for the "brief regulations," they were established because the group of six monks stayed in the same room as a householder.
Among them was a bhikṣu who,
with a distracted mind, fell asleep and his body became exposed;
for his sake, they disciplined and restrained him.
The Buddha established a rule prohibiting co-residence.

Regarding the statement that the rule was subsequently relaxed through formal proposal (*naya*), it refers to the subsequent occasion when, due to Rāhula, the permission to stay for two or three nights was granted. Question:
Since the Buddha did not permit staying overnight with those who were not fully ordained,
Rāhula should have complied with this instruction by being expelled;
why then was he rebuked?
[The opponent] says: "A foolish person lacks compassion and does not protect my feelings. [The respondent] answers:
"When a disciple has a matter to attend to, it is only right that they consult and inform [their teacher]."
The Buddha permitted such actions only due to specific circumstances;
to drive them out so abruptly violates the etiquette of a disciple and is an extreme lack of compassion.
Therefore, the Buddha rebuked the deluded person as having no compassionate kin.
If even a son of the Buddha does not regard them with compassion,
how much less could others possibly have any loving-kindness or pity for them?
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, the Buddha rebuked a foolish person, saying:
"How can a jackal drive away a lion?
This was said because he praised the observance of the precepts while permitting [monks] to stay for two nights with those who were not yet fully ordained.
Regarding the third point, the detailed regulation, that which is explained below is it:

"If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not received full ordination for more than two nights, reaching a third night, it is a pāyattika. This complete precept text consists of four phrases.
1. An offender; 2. One who has not yet received full ordination;
3. Staying overnight together beyond the limit.
There are four offenses.
The first phrase is self-evident.
The second refers to "one who has not received full ordination."
Excluding bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it refers to those who have not yet received the full ordination (upasaṃpadā).
Regarding the three instances of "staying overnight together," the Vinaya states:
There are four types of staying overnight in the same room,
as previously explained; among these,
there are distinctions according to the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Two people in one room is one case;
two rooms with one person each is another;
three people in one room is yet another.
The four types of rooms are all distinct;
these are all included within the category of "staying together.
Regarding the statement that "exceeding two nights and reaching three nights," this refers to the limit of the allowance as stated in the Vinaya.
If one stays overnight for up to three nights, one should rise before the first light of dawn appears and depart;
if it reaches the fourth night,
one must leave of one's own accord.
If he causes him to leave,
or if he does not avoid the appearance of light and instead gives rise to the perception of light, then by the dawn of the fourth day, he commits one *pāyattika* offense;
if he avoids the appearance of light, he has not committed an offense at the time of dawn, even on the fourth night.
For every time one turns over while staying overnight, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Since the current *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* directly addresses the violation without avoiding the specific details of the transgression,
it states that exceeding two nights and reaching three nights constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If one avoids the appearance of light and passes through the third night without having committed an offense by the fourth night,

according to the *Jìzhù*, if one has completed the offense on the third night and has not yet repented, there is no allowance for two nights; rather, one incurs the offense of *sui-xu* (staying with others) immediately upon the completion of the third night.
If the confession is completed, one may stay for two nights.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one sits through the night,
or if one is ill, it is permitted to stay overnight with a śrāmaṇera or with a sick person who is lying down.
Other healthy bhikṣus should not lie down.
Regarding the four terms "pāyattika," these are the names for the offenses.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"If it reaches the third night and the bhikṣu has no place to go, he should not lie down or sit until the appearance of the dawn light."
If one has reached the fourth watch of the night and there is no place to go when the dawn is about to appear,
if one goes by oneself.
If one sends them away, or if one does not do so, one commits a *thullaccaya* offense.
If one stays together with a male non-human or an animal for more than three nights, it is all a *dukkaṭa*; other circumstances for non-offenses are the same as in the preceding precept.
The Sixth [Precept]: Reciting the Precepts Together with One Who Has Not Received Full Ordination.
Regarding the intent of the prohibition, according to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya*, the Buddha established this precept for four reasons:
first, to distinguish [the Buddhist community] from non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*).
Second, because there is a distinction between the positions of teacher and disciple;
third, because it distinguishes and clarifies speech;
fourth, because it relies on the actual meaning rather than valuing mere sounds. There are five distinct conditions.
First, the Dharma taught by the Buddha;
second, the words, phrases, and meanings;
third, those who are not yet fully prepared.
Fourth, one commits an offense by reciting in unison with others.
Fifth, one commits an offense as soon as the words are clearly articulated.
Below, the core text of the precepts (*śīla-sūtra*) is explained.
This precept was established because the group of six bhikṣus, while in the lecture hall with various elders,
recited the words of the sūtras in loud voices,
thereby disturbing the bhikṣus who were practicing meditation.
The Buddha then established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu recites together with a person who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika offense.
This complete text of the precept consists of four phrases.
1. An offender; 2. One who has not yet received full ordination;
3. One who recites together.
There are four offenses.
The first two phrases are self-evident.
Regarding the third, it refers to the practice of chanting together.
"Reciting together" means reciting names and phrases neither before nor after, but simultaneously.
"Chanting together" refers to both types of recitation—whether copying [the text] from the beginning or from the end—and these are both termed "reciting together.
As for what is called "Dharma":
Whatever is spoken by the Buddha, whatever is spoken by the śrāvakas, whatever is spoken by the ṛṣis, and whatever is spoken by the devas—all these are the True Dharma.
Regarding the four-word offense of pāyattika:
this constitutes a transgression of the precepts.
Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"If the Śrāvaka disciples or others speak [a teaching] that is approved by the Buddha, it is then called the Dharma."
If this Dharma is recited by skipping either the preceding or the succeeding portions, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
Therefore, the Vinaya states:
"Regarding those who recite together..."
This refers to reciting the meaning of phrases,
the meaning of words and syllables,
and likewise that which is not the meaning of phrases.
Regarding the meaning of "words and phrases" (*padārtha*):
when two people recite together with identical sounds and identical phrasing, the three modes of conduct (*tri-īryāpatha*) are expressed;
because their principles are the same, it is termed "the meaning of words and phrases."
This constitutes a *thullaccaya* offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong lü) states:
"If the voices are synchronized but the phrases differ, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
Regarding the phrase "not the meaning of the sentence":
while the former person has not yet finished saying, "Commit no evil," the latter person copies what preceded.
To say "commit no evil" implies that the preceding instruction fails to manifest the perfection of right practice; therefore,
it is said to be "not the meaning of the phrase."
This also constitutes an offense of *thullaccaya*,
because the words are identical and the sounds are connected.
As for the meaning of the words and phrases:
The phrases express the principle of impermanence;
they provide all-encompassing benefit for the enlivening of the spirit.
This is called "phrase-flavor" (jùwèi).
To excerpt and seize upon the preceding words results in an incomplete expression of principles, providing no basis for the functioning of the spirit;
therefore, it is said that these are not "sentence-meanings" (*pada-artha*). As for "word-meanings" (*vyañjana-artha*):
Chanting in unison and reciting together expresses the name and its essence;
when the principle is perfected, it is called the meaning of the word.
To excerpt and seize upon the preceding words renders the name and essence incomplete.
Therefore, it is said that this is not the literal meaning. The *Jianlun* (Treatise on Seeing) states:
"The entire Vinaya Piṭaka, Abhidharma Piṭaka, and Sūtra Piṭaka were spoken by the Buddha."
Later, when the five hundred arhats held the council,
they all recited this dharma together and were found to have committed *thullaccaya* offenses.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, for each individual category, chapter, or section, one incurs a *pācittiya* transgression.
If one composes texts according to one's own intent, even including secular writings,
there is no offense because they were not spoken by the Buddha; this is included among the non-offenses.
The Vinaya states:
"One should say, 'I have finished speaking; you speak now.
If one person recites until the end and another writes it down," so it is said.
If two people share the same practice and recite together,
even if they mistakenly say "this" for "that" or vice versa,
neither commits an offense.
The Seventh Precept: Prohibiting the disclosure of another’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) to one who has not received full ordination.
The intention behind this regulation is that the monastic community ought to be pure and distinguished;
when its reputation for excellence spreads abroad, it inspires faith in the teachings among the people.
If a monk speaks of such coarse and evil matters to laypeople,
and those people hear them, they will develop a sense of indifference and disregard toward that Jewel of the Sangha.
One loses the sense of reverence, faith, and veneration;
the damage is profound.
Therefore, a sacred regulation must be established. There are seven specific conditions [for this].
First, a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī;
second, having committed an offense of the first two categories;
third, knowing that one has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya).
Fourth, there must be no legal grounds for the absence of the Saṃgha;
fifth, one must speak to a person who has not yet received full ordination;
sixth, the words spoken must be clear and intelligible.
Seventh, the preceding section has been heard and understood.
Below, the actual text of the precept (śikṣāpada) is clearly explained.
This precept was established because the group of six bhikṣus (ṣaḍvargika) spoke of their offenses involving saṃghāvaśeṣa to laypeople.
When a bhikṣu committed an offense beyond that limit, he felt shame only upon hearing the voice [of others].
The other bhikṣus informed the Buddha,
and the Buddha then established the precept.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination, except by means of a formal act of the Saṃgha (saṃghakamma), this constitutes a pāyattika offense. This complete precept text consists of five phrases.
1. One who is an offender;
2. one who knows it is a grave offense;
3. one who speaks to a person who has not yet received the precepts.
Fourth, the removal [of the offense] through a formal monastic act (*saṃghakarma*).
Fifth, the determination of the offense.
The first phrase is self-evident.
Regarding the second phrase, "knowing that another has committed a coarse offense," the Vinaya states:
"Committing offenses belonging to the first two categories [of the Prātimokṣa] is termed a coarse and evil offense (*sthūlātyaya*)."
Regarding the third phrase, "speaking to one who has not yet received the precepts," the Vinaya states:
"This refers to anyone other than bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs."
The fourth phrase, "except by formal monastic authorization (saṃgha-kamma)," is the text that provides an exception.
The fifth phrase states "an offense of expiation (pāyattika)."
This constitutes a transgression of the precepts.
Thus, the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* states:
"It would be better to destroy a stupa or damage an image than to speak of another's grave offense."
If one destroys a Buddha stūpa, the offense has a limit;
however, to speak of another’s grave offense (sthūlātyaya) is an offense that destroys the Dharma-body, equal in gravity to the five heinous crimes (ānantarya).
Thus, the Vinaya says:
